versions.body:
# Character IN-list Coercion and Shared Sorting Proposal

Character IN-list coercion and Shared row sorter are initially placed in a single proposal. They may not belong to the same implementation; their only common point right now is that both get stuck at the optimizer handoff boundary: when list literals acquire a shape usable for index selection, and under what conditions the existing sorter continues to be reused. The old investigation leads to `sql/analyzer/costed_index_scan.go`. The file belongs to `package analyzer`, but this is only a starting point for tracing back, not enough to assign the two to the same object.

The initial working assumption was simple: character values in the list look similar to ordinary strings, so perhaps existing string handling can be reused; since the sorter is already shared, there may be no need to revisit it in the new plan branch. This assumption is convenient, but it conflates two unconfirmed premises: whether the appearance of a literal can stand in for its declared type, and whether "shared" already means that row shape and sort conditions can pass through unchanged.

Don't turn this into a generalized conversion rule here yet. The proposal does only two small things: isolate the point at which list members enter range construction; and treat reuse of Shared row sorter as an existing constraint, rather than as an exit created to support list conversion. The former requires knowing the relationship between the declared SQL type and the literal members; the latter requires knowing whether there are additional row-shape requirements before and after the call. When neither side has a conclusion, they should not be bundled into the same change just because they are adjacent in the path.

## Parked Branches

Two approaches that could easily lead us astray are noted here first. One is to choose the string branch solely based on whether the literal is quoted; this avoids the type handoff but does not answer when the declared type takes effect. The other is to defer list conversion until the sorting phase; this may appear to eliminate one handoff, but the sorter does not inherently own list semantics. Both can serve as counterexamples when tracing back, but should not go directly into this trial.

The review questions left in the margin of the old page still stand:

- If a character list is treated as an ordinary string at an earlier point, what can the later index-cost assessment still see;
- If some numeric checks are affected by string handling, should the fast path stop;
- When the sorter is used by multiple callers, who can decide the row shape it receives.

The provisional trial direction is to first have the list side provide a stable range input, then check whether costed index scan consumes only this kind of input; on the sorting side, keep the existing Shared row sorter and do not create a second sorting path solely for this trial. If the conversion point must depend on the sorter's internal state, or if list handling changes numeric semantics that should be preserved, drop the idea of closing out both in the same round and handle them separately.

## Stop Point for This Round

This round accepts only one small success signal: list handling does not require the sorter to interpret members on its behalf, and sorter reuse does not force list handling to rewrite the original input. If these two conditions cannot both be made clear, leave the original call and original issue in place; do not make a combined commit.

Not yet spelled out: whether character types need the same entry point, which layer passes the members' type information to range construction, and whether the boundary of the shared sorter is constrained only by the caller.

# Character IN-list Coercion and Shared Sorting Proposal

The previous version put Character IN-list coercion and the Shared row sorter together simply because both stalled at the optimizer handoff. This version keeps that starting point but no longer treats "reviewed in the same pass" as "implemented in the same place." List-member interpretation, range construction, and sorter reuse are three separable issues; only once the first two can be explained is it worth continuing the discussion of costed index selection.

## The Original Draft Remains

> If list members look like ordinary strings, send them through the existing string handling first; since Shared row sorter already has existing call sites, do not create a separate sorting path for the list issue.

This was a working assumption from 2023, not a confirmed rule. It skipped the question of whether a member's textual form is equivalent to its declared type. It also skipped whether the shared sorter still receives the original row shape. The draft's benefit was narrowing the focus from a broad optimizer topic to lists and sorting; its drawback was leaving two unknowns in the same sentence.

The `sql/analyzer/costed_index_scan.go` referenced by the old investigation is still a useful point for follow-up. The beginning of the file shows `package analyzer` and the import section, which can help trace range handling near the costed index scan. The follow-up provides no evidence about sorter ownership and does not show that list members should be interpreted by the sorter. The file location therefore remains navigation only; it cannot continue to serve as the rationale for a combined approach.

The original draft also treated the formation of a range as meaning that later selection could make up for the earlier interpretation. We are no longer using that order after review. Selection can compare only candidates that have already been formed; it cannot go back and decide the member's declared type. This remains a working judgment for now, but it is sufficient to review the list and sorter separately.

## Two Candidates After the Follow-Up

There are two candidates on the list side. The first routes members into string handling based on their literal appearance. Its advantage is one fewer type handoff; its drawback is that it does not make clear where the declared type takes effect. The second preserves the member's declared SQL type when the member enters range construction and leaves the conversion issue on the list side. The second introduces one more boundary to review, but it does not require later index cost selection to interpret the input for it.

| Candidate | Benefit available at the time | Gap left behind |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Route by literal appearance | Short path; existing string handling can continue to be tried | Cannot explain why the same appearance should be treated the same under different declared types |
| Hand off the type before the range | Makes the interpretation point for list members clear | The source material is not yet organized well enough to cover all character cases |

The second is the direction retained in this version, but it is not final behavior. Here, "retain the type" only means that review can trace how a member enters range construction. It does not presuppose a function name or move all string-related handling into one place.

## The Short-Circuit Crossed Out

> First let the string path pass the member downstream; if index cost does not accept it, let the later selection drop it.

This section was marked deprecated after being moved here from the old draft. The downstream stage can choose among existing candidates; it cannot make up the member's interpretation for the upstream stage. In particular, when string handling may affect numeric decisions, simply saying "the later stage will drop it" is not enough to show that the input still retains its original meaning. The old section remains so that the same omission is not mistaken for a new proposal during the next follow-up.

## Position of the Shared Row Sorter

The proposal on the sorting side is much narrower than the one on the list side: keep reusing the existing Shared row sorter, and do not turn it into a conversion path for list members. If a candidate requires it to receive a different row shape, that is a new boundary that must be described separately, not a benefit of sharing. There is currently no material supporting a new sorter, nor any material supporting hiding type information in sorting state.

Three formulations were compared at the time. Keeping the existing calls is the default; creating a new sorting path to try for lists is discussed only if there is an actual row-shape change; deferring type conversion until immediately before sorting is excluded from the trial. This leaves the two small issues waiting for their own evidence, but it makes it easier to see which side is at fault than having the sorter interpret the list for it.

From this version onward, "string handling" is only the name of a candidate path; it is no longer used as a synonym for the member's semantics having been determined. "Shared sorter" likewise describes only the existing reuse relationship; it no longer implies that the sorter can take over arbitrary input. Narrowing these two terms is the most practical change after the follow-up.

## Gaps Left by One Review

The actual follow-up was sufficient only to confirm that the old path is still worth examining. It was not sufficient to organize a reusable sample covering a list member, its declared type, and the subsequent range input. Without all three, any claim that "all character values can continue through string handling" remains an assumption. The review also did not show that the shared sorter needs to take over conversion; it supports only retaining the existing calls for now.

The next step written in the review margin is deliberately narrow: bring back the representation of one member before it enters range construction, together with its declared type, then separately confirm whether the sorter call requires a new row shape. Do not infer that the earlier type handling is correct merely because a final plan appears workable.

## Withdrawal Line for This Trial

This round can continue only if the list side can explain the member's type handoff outside the sorter, and the sorting side can preserve the existing calls without receiving a row shape temporarily rewritten for this purpose. If either condition fails, withdraw the plan to advance the two issues together: leave the list issue at the range boundary and the sorting issue at the existing call site.

Not yet decided:

- Which layer provides the member's declared type;
- Whether character types require exactly the same handling;
- When the sorter side counts as having a new row-shape requirement.

versions.body:
# Character IN-list and Shared Sorting Proposal

This proposal has always kept Character IN-list coercion and Shared row sorter on the same page, without describing them as the same implementation. The former asks where list members acquire the types that range construction can use; the latter asks which layer must still preserve the row shape when an existing sorter continues to be used across plans. The two were initially placed together because both arise at optimizer handoff points, not because one object can replace the other. Several later addenda did not erase this starting point: it still explains why the old draft discussed both the string branch and the sorter, yet never proposed a combined change.

This page does not cover all optimizer behavior either. Each update retains only what could be clearly stated at the time about the boundary between the two objects: the handoff of list member types, the use of range inputs by costed index selection, and ensuring that existing sorter calls are not changed by mistake. This makes it possible to distinguish old assumptions from requirements tightened later.

## Initial Juxtaposition in 2023

The earliest record stated only a convenient assumption: when list members look like strings, continue treating them as strings for now, and wait until costed index scan sees the input before deciding whether it is worth proceeding; since Shared row sorter is already being called, leave it unchanged for now. At the time, this wording mistook "can continue passing it downstream" for "the semantics are already correct," and "a shared object already exists" for "there is no need to ask about boundaries." It is retained here because several later debates began with these two omissions.

An earlier investigation led readers to `sql/analyzer/costed_index_scan.go`. The visible file header contained only `package analyzer` and the import section. The old record briefly treated this location as grounds for assigning both issues to costed index scan; that position was later revised. The path can help locate where lists, range, and cost-based selection sit next to one another, but it cannot establish ownership of the sorter, much less prove that conversion of literal members has already been completed in this file.

There were three unfinished questions in the margin of the original page. First, when a literal's written form differs from its declared type, who is responsible for ensuring that range construction sees the latter. Second, if a member that looks like a string would encounter a numeric check, whether it can still go directly through the string branch. Third, when reusing a sorter, whether the caller still supplies the original row shape. They had no answers; they only limited subsequent verification to lists, types, and sorting.

In the initial draft, "the same round" referred only to review order: first check whether the list can supply the input, then check whether the sorter can remain unchanged. It never required the same commit or the same ownership. Only when this phrase was later read as a combined implementation did the boundaries of both range construction and the sorter become blurred.

The initial draft also framed this question as a one-way flow, as though, once a range had been formed, later selection would fill in the missing explanation for the earlier steps. This ordering was not accepted after review. Selection can compare existing ranges, but it cannot go back and decide the declared types for members; at the time, this distinction was only a working assumption and had not yet become a formal requirement on this page.

## First Addendum After Review

The review did not accept the arrangement to "merge first, then examine the differences." The addendum split the trial into two tracks: the list side must first explain how the input is interpreted; the sorting side is only allowed to preserve sharing relationships that already exist. "Preserve" has a narrow meaning here: it does not mean that the sorter takes responsibility for type conversion, nor does it mean that any plan node can be replaced with it.

The counterexample recorded at the time was not a specific query, but an easily overlooked pattern: members that appear in the same character form may require different conversions because their declared types differ. When the original input is not retained together with its type, a later cost-based choice cannot validate the earlier interpretation, even if it yields a viable branch. This counterexample was cited repeatedly later, but the earliest record did not describe it as a confirmed failure.

The side note on the sorter went no further than this: the shared object can continue to serve as a constraint on existing calls; if making the list trial pass requires it to accept a different row shape, that indicates the two problems should not be solved in the same change. This restriction may seem conservative, but it prevents the list's semantic issues from being hidden in the sorting path.

There was also an undeleted stop condition in the review margin: when a member's type provenance cannot be clearly explained, stop expanding the scope of the trial, and do not use a plan selected later to retroactively validate the earlier processing. This stop condition did not specify a particular API, nor did it claim that a definite error had already been found; it merely prevented the draft from filling gaps where input was missing with default strings.

## The 2024 Recheck

The second version rechecked the old navigation. `sql/analyzer/costed_index_scan.go` was still the entry point adjacent to costed index selection, and the analyzer package containing the file had not changed either; the recheck did not establish relationships such as "conversion is performed by the sorter" or "the sorter is created by the range builder." Therefore, the previous version's proposal to merge the two did not gain stronger support; instead, the two should be separated more clearly.

Two approaches were compared on the list side at the time. One selected a branch based on a member's appearance: if its textual form looked like a string, it was sent for string processing. The other carried the declared SQL type to the point where list members enter range construction, and only then decided how to interpret each member. The former was shorter to write, while the latter added an explicit type handoff; however, the latter at least did not treat the input's appearance as a conclusion about its type. The second version listed the latter as a candidate, without declaring it to be behavior that had already been implemented.

What this recheck revealed was not a new result, but a missing handoff point in the old assumption. Retaining the type up to the point before members enter range construction does not mean that all members will produce the same result; it only requires that the same layer be able to see the information needed to make the judgment. This distinction was not stated in the old draft, causing "string processing" to be treated as both a data representation and a semantic rule.

The candidate on the sorting side was even smaller in scope: continue using Shared row sorter, without adding a new set of sorting outputs for this list processing for now. The cost of doing so is that any proposal requiring a change to the row shape cannot be approved simply on the grounds of "sharing"; the benefit is that an as-yet-unverified conversion will not be inserted into the sorter. There were no performance results here, and reuse itself was not treated as evidence of correctness.

The follow-up review also ruled out an approach that seemed to offer a middle ground: first convert members into an untyped intermediate form, then add types once index candidates appear. This adds a layer of objects compared with routing directly based on text, but interpretation is still deferred. Once the candidate range loses the declared types, the later stage can only choose among results; it cannot recover why a member was interpreted that way. This compromise was not explored further.

The "trials" that year did not require both sides to be changed in one pass either. The minimum goal of the list trial was to let reviewers identify where interpretation takes place; the minimum goal of the sorting trial was to confirm that reuse did not require a new row shape. If either goal was not met, changes should stop near the original call rather than turning the other object into a patch.

### Retained old shortcut, now deprecated

> As long as list members can be passed as strings, let the string fast path handle them first; subsequent index costs will eliminate unsuitable cases. If the sorter already has a call, make no separate assessment.

The addendum from 2024 marked this passage as no longer applicable. Cost-based selection only chooses among existing inputs; it cannot restore the type information that list members lost before entering range construction. Likewise, an existing sorting call cannot replace an assessment of row shape. This passage is retained not to reinstate it, but to show readers why "can be passed" was later no longer treated as "can be adopted." The correction appears in the current conclusion later on this page, and the old text is no longer a basis for implementation.

"Subsequent" in the old passage referred to costed index selection at the time, not to an arbiter that could replace type assessment. Retaining the original word reminds readers that the issue was not whether the string path was fast, but that it was being used to answer a question that was not its responsibility.

## The gap left in 2025

Later material from the field described the gap more concretely. After the capacity review in 2025, month 9, the record for GMS-202 stopped because the original input from before the failure was missing. As a result, all that could be distinguished at the time were the failure stage and the downloadable artifacts; that material could not be used to infer exactly what declared type a particular list member had before conversion. This pause matters: it refuted the idea that "a single failure record is enough to fill in the type rules," but did not reject the proposal to continue work on type boundaries.

The gap in the material does not mean that nothing was available at the time. At least the capacity review left separate records of the stage where the check failed and the downloadable artifacts, helping readers avoid misinterpreting the existence of artifacts as evidence that the preceding stage had no problems. What was missing was the original input from an earlier point; without it, the declared type of a specific member could not be reconstructed, nor could this one case establish that all string branches were the same.

During the same period, GMS-219 used the existing call to Shared row sorter as the starting point for reproducing the behavior, focusing on whether completion would leave any additional visible changes. This shows that there is indeed an existing path on the sorter side that needs to be preserved, but it does not show that the sorter should be responsible for list conversion. The two cards now serve only as navigation aids: one preserves the evidence to distinguish when checking the character list, and the other preserves the starting point for the shared sorter call. They do not merge the two objects under a single maintainer or into a single piece of code.

This batch of records also corrects an easy-to-misread timeline. Questions about the boundary between type handling and range construction came first; the evidence gap left by the capacity review came later. The fact that the sorter was already shared came first; the request to reproduce from the pre-call state came later. We cannot reverse the order and interpret the pause on the cards as a failure caused by the sorter, nor interpret the sorter's reproduction requirement as meaning that the character list already has a complete sample.

When the original input before failure is unavailable, do not fabricate a "representative" member on the page to stand in for it. If the next review is to discuss a particular branch, it must bring back at least the list member, the declared type, and the state before it enters range construction. If only artifacts or failure-stage information remain, this page can still only remain a proposal; it cannot disguise an old working assumption as a conclusion.

## Matters Not Merged at the Review Table

Subsequent reviews narrowed the debate to two judgments that cannot replace each other. One concerns what information should be used to interpret a literal member. The other concerns the conditions under which the shared sorter preserves its existing behavior. The former belongs to the handoff from list to range; the latter belongs to continued use of the sorting object. Both are related to the optimizer, but they have no common shortcut entry point.

The review notes preserved three questions rather than three conclusions:

- "Does 'member looks like a string' refer to the literal text, or to the declared SQL type?"
- Before costed index selection sees range, who has already decided how to interpret the member?
- If Shared row sorter needs a different row shape, should it be removed from this list change?

The first candidate once tried to branch directly from the raw text. Its appeal was that it did not require passing additional type information; its drawback was that the interpretation rules depended on appearance. That is exactly why the old short-circuit was crossed out. The second candidate placed the type handoff near range builder. It added a location that had to be made explicit, but kept list semantics where the list is processed. The third candidate delayed conversion until before sorting; it merely used the existing object to mask the gap, and the review did not list it as an option to try.

The review record ultimately preserved the ordering, not a comprehensive ruling: first keep the type issue on the list side, then let cost-based selection process the range once it has been formed; the sorter should not take over conversion. This ordering neither specified a new function name nor required the shared object to take on more work. It only separated the three judgments conflated in the old draft and returned them to their respective places.

Therefore, when discussing whether reuse is possible, the answer should be whether the existing call can be maintained, not whether some new member can be sorted. When discussing whether an index can be used, the answer is whether cost-based selection can consume the range, not whether the string's appearance is already equivalent to the type. Only after answering the two questions separately can the two objects on the same page both make it through review.

The proposal for the Shared row sorter is narrowed accordingly here: retain the existing shared calls, do not add a dedicated sorter for type issues, and do not make the sorter the place where list membership is determined. If it turns out that the existing calls must change the row shape, first withdraw the sorting portion from this proposal rather than change the list rules to preserve "Shared" in the name. This way, sorter reuse can still be checked independently, and list conversion will not be tied to it.

## Adjacent items not yet split out

DOC-16 continues to cover the issues of Partial-index predicate lifecycle and Heap Top-N ownership. These are adjacent to the sorting subject discussed here, but this page does not use the Shared row sorter to determine the continued existence of partial-index predicates, nor does it decide ownership for the Top-N heap. The old draft described "sorting" too broadly, as though any plan involving ordering could be included along the way; that wording was crossed out in the addendum for the year 2024.

One adjacent issue remains here: when the list side has already provided ranges available for selection while the sorting side still uses shared calls, the two should not be covertly coupled through ad hoc row-shape conversions. There is not enough material now to refine this into an interface rename or a new call sequence. This issue remains a checkpoint for review, not a third option awaiting implementation.

This question is retained because it can prevent the two subjects from becoming entangled through ad hoc adaptation, not because the available material proves that they are already entangled. If subsequent material shows that there is indeed a boundary between them, first clearly describe the subjects at that boundary, then decide whether this issue needs to be moved off this page.

## Current scope

The current proposal only tightens the behavioral requirements for character lists to verifiable boundaries:

The IN-list range builder must support CHAR and VARCHAR operands by converting literal members with the declared SQL type, producing a MySQL range collection for costed index selection, and declining the string fast path when numeric coercion would change MySQL semantics.

This sentence breaks down the previously vague term "string processing". The objects being converted are literal members, and the basis for the decision is the declared SQL type; the range builder produces a collection for use by costed index selection. It does not claim that every IN-list will select an index, nor does it elevate cost-based selection into a type interpreter. When numeric conversion would change MySQL semantics, the original shortcut based only on the string's appearance cannot serve as an alternative entry point.

It also grounds the previously broad term "character types" in two objects that can be reviewed. List members do not acquire meaning only just before sorting; the range collection is not some general-purpose cache either, and is within the scope of this proposal only as input to costed index selection. This does not extend to other predicates, other indexing strategies, or all string processing.

The Shared row sorter portion has not been assigned a new type-related responsibility. The current arrangement is to retain the existing shared calls and treat this as an independent constraint after the list side has finished interpreting the input. In other words, list member conversion does not borrow state from the sorter; nor does the sorter gain permission to rewrite member meanings merely because it is shared. This may still require checking the calls on both sides separately, but it does not require an object that has not yet been confirmed to take responsibility for two boundaries.

The facts retained on the sorter side are similarly limited: existing calls continue to retain Shared row sorter. It can serve as a reference during review to check whether changes cross the boundary, but the name alone cannot establish where responsibility for list conversion, range construction, or index costing belongs. If dedicated row-shape adaptation is needed later, first document the need for that adaptation separately, rather than quietly changing the meaning of the shared object.

The trade-offs in this combined proposal are clear. Conversion based on the declared type requires retaining more type information than routing based on the literal's appearance, but it places semantic decisions where the list members are visible. Retaining the shared sorter gives up the convenience of "creating a sorting exit for the new branch while we are at it", in exchange for keeping existing calls unaffected by the list trial. Neither is a judgment about which file owns something; `sql/analyzer/costed_index_scan.go` remains only an entry point for checking back on adjacency relationships around costed index selection.

The withdrawal conditions also apply only to the way this proposal places the two tracks side by side. If the declared type is unavailable at the range builder, neither the string fast path nor the sorter's internal state may be used to pretend to fill that gap; the list side should stop at the existing boundary and wait for material that can explain the input. If retaining Shared row sorter requires changing the row shape of existing calls, the sorter side should be separated from this proposal, preserving the original calls rather than hiding the changes within the character-list work. The former does not permit downgrading the existing MySQL semantics, and the latter does not permit using "shared" to cover parts whose ownership remains undetermined.

## Before the two tracks meet again

The list side does not need a generalized type cross-reference table; the review still needs to answer one specific question: when each literal member reaches the range builder, is its declared type still visible? If the answer is no, we cannot directly declare the current arrangement implemented; we should first fill in the handoff point, and only then discuss the cost tradeoff. The missing input before the failure in the preceding material is exactly why this step cannot be skipped.

The sorting side only checks whether the existing Shared row sorter continues to meet the expectations of the original call. The reproduction starting point described above is suitable for recording this: start from the state before the call and check whether any additional observable change occurs after completion. If a change exists, first describe whether it belongs to the row shape, the sorting condition, or another object; do not automatically attribute it to list conversion. This does not require the sorter to prove the correctness of the character list.

The order of these two things cannot be reversed. First pass list members, with their known types, to range construction, then let costed index selection make its own choice on the resulting collection; the shared sorter continues to serve as a constraint on the other existing call chain. The page does not specify a function name, call sequence, or new sorting implementation for this, because the existing material does not support those details.

If the original input is retrieved later, it should be used to distinguish which layer already has information, not to rewrite the draft from the year 2023. Old assumptions remain as old assumptions; new material only determines whether a candidate can move forward. This way, the next revision will not incorrectly write the time when the gap disappeared as if the problem had never existed.

## Appendix: Old Examples Were Not Deleted

### Purpose of the Old Navigation

The old navigation entry is still `sql/analyzer/costed_index_scan.go`. Its original purpose was to look back from around costed index selection at the handoff between the list and range. The withdrawn inference was that finding the file meant that the Shared row sorter's responsibility was there as well. This navigation line is retained so that later readers can return to the original lookup location, not to restore that attribution.

**Old example one: borrowing the string branch based on appearance.** An early draft treated "members written in character form" as sufficient reason to enter the string fast path, and hoped that cost selection would naturally exclude unsuitable ranges. This example is now used only to explain the old judgment: it did not record the declared type, nor did it explain where to stop when numeric semantics were affected. Do not copy it back as implementation steps; the correction should follow the currently finalized list boundary.

**Old example two: the shared object automatically absorbing a new row shape.** Another old example described the Shared row sorter as able to serve any new planned branch as a side effect, as long as it was used by an existing call. It overlooked that the caller might still depend on the original row shape, and it incorrectly described the sorting object as the endpoint of list conversion. This example is likewise retained because it explains why the sorting section later promised only to preserve sharing, not to promise to complete the list work.

Neither of the two old examples in the appendix has a corresponding complete original failing input. They are not suitable for fabricating additional test cases, nor can they be used to infer the Partial-index predicate lifecycle or Heap Top-N ownership. What is still missing is a review using the original members and declared types, along with confirmation of whether the existing sorting calls introduce any additional observable changes; until then, the current behavioral requirements and the shared sorter's boundaries should be maintained separately.

# Troubleshooting partial indexes and Heap Top-N

After an index definition changes, if the original filter takes a different plan path, or result differences appear only when sorting and a limit are both present, don't combine the two into a single failure yet. The earliest records only confirmed that the symptoms appeared around these two entry points; there was no conclusion at the time about where the predicate had passed through in between.

## Initial triage

```text
Plan or result changes observed
├─ Immediately after an index definition change
│  ├─ Save the index objects before and after the change, and the query filter
│  ├─ Check whether the index is still identifiable in the plan
│  └─ If the predicate's path is unclear, stop at the index branch
└─ Only when sorting and a limit are both present
   ├─ Compare the rows fed into the sorter with the rows ultimately returned
   └─ If they don't match, stop at the Heap Top-N branch
```

For the index branch, first retain the objects, filter, and plan fragments based on the same initial state. If the plan did not select the index, record only that it was not selected; don't infer from this that the predicate has disappeared. If the final plan still mentions the index, the earliest approach was to treat the predicate as a selection issue unless it could be shown to have changed at an earlier point.

Open the sorting branch only when sorting and a limit are both present. The question here is whether the rows received and returned by the heap still look like the same set of rows. Without evidence at both boundaries, don't attribute the output difference to the heap or use it to explain why the index was selected.

To keep the investigation moving at the time, a narrowly scoped provisional rule was adopted: if the final plan still showed the index, stop tracing the predicate for the time being; set aside samples containing Heap Top-N. This rule only kept the two investigation tickets apart. It did not prove that the two paths were unrelated.

## Stop conditions

Stop comparing if the before-and-after objects are not based on the same initial state, or if the filter and the sort/limit are not from the same query. Don't fill in the intermediate process from a plan excerpt alone.

Two questions remain open: after an index definition change, does the predicate change only during planning; and does the row shape before and after Heap Top-N need to be recorded separately?

# Partial Index and Heap Top-N Investigation

The earliest note split index selection from sorting with a limit. A review found that repeatedly rereading one plan fragment does not show where the two paths diverge. The investigation below still follows the old entry point, but spells out what each judgment actually requires. If any one item is missing, the branch stops at that gap; do not guess at an intermediate state.

## Record four fields first during review

For each sample, record four fields in the same order:

- the index object before the change, and the state used when the query started;
- the adjusted index definition or the ALTER INDEX that triggered the change;
- the query's filters, sort conditions, and limit;
- the visible plan fragment, or the rows that can be compared before and after the sort path.

The four fields are not meant to be turned into a polished table. They prevent the filters from one query from being combined with the output from another. If the objects before the change differ, or the query itself has changed its filters, the later comparison has no common baseline and should be recorded separately.

## Index side

If the behavior appears immediately after an index definition or ALTER INDEX, first check whether the predicate is actually visible in the sample. If the definition does not retain it and the final plan does not either, the index name alone cannot show which segment lost it. If the index is visible in the final plan but the filter appears only in another text segment, do not combine the two text segments into a single conclusion.

If the plan did not choose the index, first record the non-selection and the filters at the time. This may be related to range, cost, or other selection factors, or the sample may simply not include the full predicate; this review does not attribute it directly to any one cause. Conversely, selecting the index does not automatically show that the predicate made it through every point that needs to be checked.

The old note treated the final plan as the stopping point. The review keeps that action but adds a constraint: terminal text can only show what remains visible at the end; it cannot establish what happened on the definition side or at intermediate handoffs. If the sample provides only terminal text, the index branch stops there.

When the query filters and index predicate look similar, preserve them as-is first. Do not remove a range, comparison operator, or compound condition just to make the two conditions identical. At this point, all that can be said is that further checking is needed; similar wording is not enough to conclude that index selection was reasonable.

## Heap Top-N side

Classify a sample under the Heap Top-N side only when sorting and a limit genuinely appear together. First retain the row shape before sorting and the shape of the rows ultimately returned. Row shape means more than the row count: it also includes which columns each row carries and the order of those columns. If both endpoints were not recorded, do not infer from the final output what the heap received.

If the difference already appears before entering the sort path, send the sample back to the upstream plan for inspection rather than continuing to call it Heap Top-N. If the row shape remains the same through the sort path but the rows ultimately returned differ, leave this branch open; whether this and the index predicate can be identified are two separate things to inspect side by side.

Some old records excluded Heap Top-N from the sample first and then discussed the index. The review did not establish that this order is reliable. Results with a sort and limit cannot answer where the predicate went for the index branch, and whether the index was selected cannot answer where the rows changed for the heap branch.

## Stop point by call name

The old investigation record points to `sql/analyzer/indexed_joins.go` by issue name and call name. The file header directly shows `package analyzer` and the import section, so it remains the entry point for locating the code adjacent to analyzer. The attempt to use it as the sole breakpoint did not work: this location does not account for both where the predicate goes next and the row shapes before and after the heap.

This path therefore has a narrow purpose on this page. Once the index branch confirms that it needs to locate the code adjacent to analyzer, it can continue from here. If the Heap Top-N branch does not land at the same place, do not force it back in just because the filename contains index. The path itself cannot supply the sample's two missing endpoints.

## Old judgments still retained

The earliest provisional judgment remains here: when the final plan still shows the index, do not trace the predicate first; put samples with a sort and limit in a separate group. It was useful for splitting up a batch of messy records, but now it only explains why the old records stopped at the terminal text.

When range or covering-index cost becomes the main issue, temporarily note the other path at DOC-17. Do not use the range or cost checks on that page here to work backward to a claim that the predicate is no longer a problem.

Two points remain unresolved: at which handoff after the definition change the predicate becomes invisible; and whether the row shapes before and after Heap Top-N can be matched from the same sample. When neither side has paired records, retain only the trigger condition.

# Partial Index and Heap Top-N Troubleshooting

When someone arrives here via an old link, they often have only a plan fragment or a set of results with ordering and a limit. After an index definition is changed, the relationship between filter conditions and index selection may look wrong, and the row-ownership issue for Heap Top-N can easily appear at the same time. The two phenomena were once filed under the same issue name, so the old records were not deleted; first place the sample on the tree below.

In the following, a condition attached to an index definition is called a predicate. Heap Top-N refers to the heap path that must be examined separately when ordering and a limit appear together; row shape means which columns a row carries and the order of those columns. Here, a single terminal plan fragment cannot substitute for the two paths before and after it.

## What to look for first

```text
A plan or result difference is observed
├─ Appears only after the index definition or ALTER INDEX
│  ├─ Keep the object from before the change, the definition after the change, and the query's filter conditions
│  ├─ Check whether the predicate is still visible at each handoff
│  └─ If they do not line up, stop first at the predicate branch
├─ Appears only when ordering and a limit are both present
│  ├─ Compare the shape of the rows sent into the sorting path with the shape of the rows ultimately retrieved
│  └─ If they do not line up, stop first at the Heap Top-N branch
└─ Both sides change
   └─ Split them into two records; do not use the sort result to draw a conclusion about the index condition
```

The stopping points in the tree do not close the issue. They only mean that the current sample has not yet put the destination of the index condition and the rows before and after the heap into a single record that can be compared. First fill in the missing side; if both sides cannot be completed, keep them as two unresolved items and do not assign ownership to either side.

When evaluating the index path, the same row count does not mean the same predicate; when evaluating the heap path, the same index name does not mean the same row shape. Each branch has its own starting point and stopping point.

## The first page from 2023

The earliest note put Partial-index predicate lifecycle and Heap Top-N ownership side by side only because they would be raised after the same query change. The working assumption at the time was narrow: if the terminal plan could still identify the modified index, the predicate was initially treated as having reached the selection point with the index; differences involving ordering and a limit were handed to the other track. This allowed people to continue reviewing the sample, but it did not explain what the predicate actually looked like from the definition through each subsequent segment.

> Old judgment, now deprecated: when the terminal plan still mentions the index, first treat the predicate as having reached the selection point with the index. Samples with ordering and a limit go elsewhere.

Very few actions from that time were retained. On the index side, we copied only the object, filter conditions, and one plan fragment under the same initial state; on the heap side, we asked only whether the rows ultimately fetched had changed. If the plan did not select the index, it was recorded as not selected, not treated as evidence that a condition had been lost. Conversely, seeing the index at the endpoint was not treated as a reusable conclusion; it only allowed the investigation to stop there at that time.

The initial draft framed Top-N as an almost purely endpoint issue. This was to keep sorting noise from obscuring the index branch, not a judgment about where the rows entered the heap. Later records did not scrub this sentence, because some old samples were retained precisely through this narrow split.

If an old sample contains only "index" or "Top-N" without the same initial object, do not merge it merely because the names are the same; it can only show that someone stopped in the same area at that time.

## The Four Boxes in the Margin of the On-Call Page

The four boxes were later added in the page margin. The format was uneven, but it remained more useful than merely forwarding the plan text: the same pre-change object, the changed index definition or ALTER INDEX plan, the filter conditions and sorting restrictions in the query, and the rows visible at the end of the plan or before and after sorting. If any box was missing, the annotation required stopping first; do not fill the gap by combining in another query.

This margin note also leaves an ambiguity that was unresolved at the time. When someone wrote "the condition is gone," it could mean that the condition was absent by definition, that it was no longer visible in a later plan, or simply that the final excerpt had omitted it. The three cases often used the same wording in the old records, so the breakpoint cannot be determined from those few words. This distinction later became the reason for correcting the old route.

The four-cell table does not need to be complete every time either. For samples without sorting or constraints, a heap edge should not be fabricated just to fill the fourth cell; for samples without definition changes, the output should not be explained using an index line. First, let the triggering condition determine which two endpoints need to be filled in.

The margin note on the sorting side is likewise incomplete. It treats row shape as optional and adds it only when the output difference is obvious; as a result, the old tables occasionally contain only the sorting condition, with no rows from before they entered the heap. For this kind of old sample, what can be established is that it once triggered the sorting branch; this does not establish which batch of rows Heap Top-N had already taken over.

## 2024 Year: Halfway Through Tracing by Call Name

A review first followed the issue name and call name in the old records. The path ultimately led to `sql/analyzer/indexed_joins.go`. The file header directly shows `package analyzer` and the import section, which is enough to lead to the area adjacent to analyzer; it does not spell out all at once the qualifying conditions for partial indexes or heap ownership. Treating this file as the sole breakpoint was the approach that did not work this time.

At the time, "index selection looks wrong" was written up as something sufficiently explained on the analyzer side. Subsequently, no handoff record was found on that path that could answer both questions at once: where the limiting condition remains identifiable, and where rows change shape under the ordering constraint. The old conclusion was not quietly changed into an affirmative statement; an unconfirmed marker was simply retained alongside it.

Therefore, the stopping point for this path is clear: it can provide an analyzer entry point, but it cannot fill in the connections between definitions, filter conditions, or row shapes for the sample. Before continuing along the path, first place the sample back on a branch of the tree.

After review, the sample was required to be split into two questions first. The first asks whether the predicate after the definition change can still be found along the subsequent path; the second asks whether the row shapes seen before and after Heap Top-N are the same. Both questions can start with the same query, but a plan fragment for the first question cannot be used to answer the second. When neither side has enough fragments, retain only the trigger conditions.

Samples involving Tuple inequality ranges or Covering-index cost choice were later recorded separately in DOC-17. That page can handle range or cost checks; here, it is not used in reverse as evidence that the predicate is already in order.

## The old route that was not deleted

The following passage is still visible in the old links. It is retained to help explain why some historical records contain only the final plan. It is no longer a set of steps to follow.

```text
Old route, deprecated
If the final plan lists an index name      → Stop tracing the predicate
If both sorting and a limit are present          → First exclude Heap Top-N from the sample
If the index is not selected              → First explain it in terms of cost or range
```

At the time, it was used to shorten on-call troubleshooting: first make a decision based on the final text, then defer the remaining questions. This ordering itself left a gap: even if a result was added later, there was no way to know which row it answered.

These three lines squeezed three different things into a single sequence. The first treated visibility at the end as a completed handoff; the second required excluding the heap first, which often left no record of the rows before and after the heap; the third preemptively explained non-selection in terms of cost or range. They can explain why old investigations stopped at a particular point, but they cannot characterize new samples.

The most troublesome aspect of the old route was not its brevity, but that it led people to skip the relationship between query filter conditions and index predicates. If the filter conditions do not satisfy the predicate, neither seeing an index nor failing to see one can be explained using those three lines. This counterexample was later written beside the old route, without deleting the original wording.

## Insert in the review notebook

The review left no unified conclusion about ownership, only two instructions. The first was written below the old route:

> First ask at which stage the predicate is lost, then ask what rows the heap receives; the second question cannot be used to answer the first.

After the meeting, a check-marked annotation elsewhere added more detail: the same initial state can be shared, but edges for plan handoffs and row shapes must be recorded separately. If only the final result is available, first return to the triggering branch; do not fill the partial-index column with guesses about Heap Top-N just to make the record look complete.

These two instructions did not answer where else to look beyond the source files, nor did they establish final ownership of the sorting path. The only change they left was to reverse the ordering in the old route: first distinguish what is being observed, then decide whether to continue tracing a particular handoff point.

The end of the insert also says: if the two tracks share only the issue name, not the same initial object, stop each track separately. This requirement does not designate anyone as the ultimate owner; it only prevents old records from borrowing each other's conclusions.

## Correction added in 2025

The correction added later did not rewrite the preceding notes; it only replaced the point that "seeing an index at the end is enough". New samples start from the same initial object and line up the expression on the definition side, the relevant plans, and the objects seen during actual execution; only then will the index branch avoid mistaking a missing excerpt for a condition having disappeared.

In the actual record, the index track must at least be able to match the same expression on the definition side and the execution side; the Heap track must at least be able to match entry into the sorting path with the rows ultimately retrieved. The two tracks may reference the same query, but the record cannot consist of just a single screenshot.

The original requirement currently retained is as follows:

> Index definitions and ALTER INDEX plans must carry an optional sql.Expression predicate through planning and execution, expose non-empty predicates through the PartialIndex contract, and select a partial index only when the query filter implies that predicate.

This sentence separates three things that were conflated in the old records: expressions in definitions or ALTER INDEX plans must remain available for handoff throughout; non-empty predicates must have an interface surface; and index selection is also constrained by the relationship between the query filter and that predicate. It gives only a necessary condition for selection, not a guarantee that "the filter condition is satisfied" means that index will necessarily be selected.

Therefore, the old route in the first half can only be used to explain old records. New samples must not skip intermediate handoffs just because an index name appears at the end, nor send the issue directly to Heap Top-N just because the plan did not select the index.

## The two current inspection tracks

When the trigger is in an index definition or ALTER INDEX, first place the predicate in the definition alongside the filter condition of the same query. If the initial objects are not the same, or the query's filter condition has changed between before and after the change, stop this comparison and collect a new paired sample. If there is no comparable expression on the definition side, record it as empty; do not add a non-empty condition for the interface surface.

If the queries before and after the change use different filter conditions, retain both filter conditions in the sample; do not assess implication across queries. Conditions that look similar in wording are not sufficient grounds for two samples to share a single selection assessment.

Next, trace that expression through the objects observed in planning and execution. If it is visible at the definition site but not at a later handoff point, record the last location where it is still visible and the first location where it is not; do not switch to discussing the heap at this point. If the predicate is empty, do not expect it to appear as a nonempty interface surface. If it is nonempty but cannot be found when handed off to the interface surface, the issue remains in the predicate branch.

When the query filter does not imply the index predicate, selecting the partial index cannot be treated as the correct path; stop assessing index selection for this sample here. If the filter implies the predicate but the plan does not select the index, do not claim, conversely, that the predicate is already wrong; range splitting, cost evaluation, or other selection factors may still be involved. Once the sample has shifted to Tuple inequality ranges or Covering-index cost choice, continue at DOC-17; do not merge the two issues into a single conclusion here.

Only open the Heap Top-N line of investigation when sorting and a limit actually appear together in the same query. First, write down the shape of the rows entering the sort path and the shape of the rows ultimately retrieved, side by side. When comparing row shapes, matching row counts alone is not enough; column presence and order must also match. If the rows have already changed shape before entering the heap, return to the upstream path that produced those rows; do not record this as an issue attributable to the heap.

If the row shape remains the same throughout and differences appear only after the heap, retain the Heap Top-N branch, while still assessing the index branch separately according to the earlier conditions. When sorting and a limit do not appear together, this page does not use the Heap Top-N label in place of the original symptom. If neither end can be obtained, do not use whether the index was selected to guess what rows the heap received.

Conversely, obtaining both ends before and after the heap cannot fill in the expression on the definition side either. Older records once treated these two gaps as canceling each other out; that is no longer how they are handled. `sql/analyzer/indexed_joins.go` can still serve as an entry point adjacent to the analyzer; whether to continue along it must be determined by the handoff points these two lines of investigation have reached.

## The side path is still waiting

The later-added GMS-203 requires reproducing the lifecycle from the state before the call and confirming whether any additional visible changes remain after completion. The contract wording in the card follows the spelling search above. The September addendum still marks one point as unconfirmed and leaves this run's input and output in cardinality comparison; this is not a result that can replace the current branch assessment.

This card was later marked as blocked while waiting for the release window for Memory indexes and table identity. Before that window, just retain the trigger conditions and existing samples; do not interpret the waiting status as meaning that the index or heap has already recovered. One question has not been split off: after the window closes, should the inputs and outputs in cardinality comparison get a separate record, or remain attached to this lifecycle? There is no answer here.

## Appendix: Two Old Examples

These two examples are not new tests, just common ways of writing things in old notes, retained for people reviewing old reports.

**Old example one, an index name at the end.** After the index definition was adjusted, the record said only that the final plan still listed a certain index, so it described the lifecycle as complete. This wording omitted the intermediate handoff and did not explain the relationship between the query filters and qualifying conditions. When you see this kind of report now, treat it as a fragment left over from the old approach, not as something to fill in as a pass.

**Old example two, treating the heap as noise first.** A sample with sorting and a limit showed a discrepancy. The record first excluded Heap Top-N from the sample, then discussed index selection. What remains in such cases is often only the output: you cannot see the rows entering the sorting path, nor tell whether the discrepancy occurred before or after the heap. This example no longer applies, but it explains why some old links put the two types of issues in the same paragraph.

The appendix does not replace the earlier triage. It only reminds readers of old records which side is missing from the final plan and the final output, respectively.

# Central conjunction splitting experiment notes

The record starts at `sql/analyzer/costed_index_scan.go`. It belongs to the `analyzer` package; old troubleshooting notes point both the problem name and call name for Central conjunction splitting to this location. This round did not treat the filename as implementation ownership; it only used it as an entry point for revisiting the boundary between the expression side and the cost side.

The Empty-statistics fallback left on the same page is there to keep two changes separate: the shape after the conditions are organized, and whether the cost path can continue when statistics are empty. Start with four columns on the lab sheet: expression input, expression-side observation, statistics state, and cost-side observation. When there is no complete plan output, do not use the latter two columns to fill in conclusions for the first two.

Fix this as the rule for checking subsequent samples:

> Conjunction splitting must use the single replaceable expression.SplitConjunction entry point; it recursively returns a left-to-right slice, preserves a non-AND expression's object identity, and is shared by analyzer and memo consumers.

During checks, first keep the input expression verbatim in the record, then write the content produced by splitting; do not infer expression processing from which cost path the caller ultimately selected. The two consumers do not need separate sample sets. First confirm that they go through the same entry point, then compare the slices, order, and objects retained for the same input; if the difference appears only in cost selection, record it as a cost-side difference.

# Projection Filter Sets and Statistics Identity Decision Record

Leave this entry under Quality & Regression for now. AtlasSQL 0.19 When closing this out, Projection-aware filter sets and Table schema statistics identity were handled as one adjacent issue. The former concerns how projected columns enter the filter set; the latter, which table/schema identity statistical results follow. Both surfaced near filtering, so the initial record did not split them into two ownership points.

There were two approaches at the time. Splitting them by object would let the projection relationship determine the filter set independently, with statistics identity handled elsewhere. Merging them by location would first push both decisions into the memory layer, then split them after the filtering regression was closed out. The latter was chosen. During closeout, we did not want the same anomaly to leave half an explanation in two places, nor did we want to require proving that both phenomena occurred together every time. If an investigation touched projection or statistics, it was first documented as a single decision issue. The condition for splitting was written only as "revisit if there is a counterexample"; no threshold was defined for how strong a counterexample had to be. The split approach was not rejected; it was simply recorded as something to revisit in the next round. Merging them did not mean it had been confirmed that they shared an implementation; at the time, only their ordering had not yet been disentangled.

Original decision:

> Filter sets are based on projected columns; table statistics are stored under the table schema identity. When the two are inconsistent, first change the decision on the memory side, without opening a separate handling path.

At the time, the projected columns were not treated as a new table/schema identity. The record described them as two side-by-side inputs: one arranges the filter set, and the other stores statistics. But once the order of the two decisions differed, they had to be folded back into memory first. This was thought to prevent the filtering regression from being explained repeatedly in different places.

The processing order was also treated as the responsibility boundary here. `memory/table.go` first takes on the combined decision; the projection side supplies the column set, and the statistics side supplies the table/schema identity. If a change only surfaced in projection, the approach at the time would still review it with the statistics identity in mind; the reverse was also true. When a regression involved both, responsibility was not assigned separately at first. table/schema was never listed separately as a decision that could be closed first; it always followed the filter set. The purpose of writing it this way was to put the set and identity in the same patch order.

The counterexamples did not change the choice at the time: if projection changed while table/schema stayed unchanged, we still started with the filter set; if statistics identity was in question while projection had not changed, we still returned to the same place. The original understanding was that as long as the phenomenon remained tied to the filtering path, handling it centrally would be faster than explaining it separately. These two examples were therefore not treated as triggers for splitting.

During verification, start from `memory/table.go`, trace through filter, projection, and table, then record the set and identity in the order above. The fact that the terms did not appear together in the wording was not considered a reason to move this out of the file; at the time, it was viewed as a gap left by the same processing block. The order recorded here matters more than whether the wording contains every term.

One question remains unanswered: if the projection set and table schema identity each appear unchanged, but the filtering result still needs an explanation, which should move off the memory side first? The original decision gave no conditions; it only said to handle them centrally for now.
