# Join and Window Boundary Troubleshooting

Regression materials often present two signals side by side: changes in the condition form of `Merge-join inequality orientation`, and abnormal state after `Window aggregate default frames` processing. Both fall within the scope of AtlasSQL 0.19 Optimizer Convergence, but "appearing in the same round" is not evidence of a shared implementation. First separate them by material type; conditions, runtime artifacts, and window state each have different stopping points.

The earlier investigation pointed to `sql/analyzer/indexed_joins.go` based on the issue name and call name. `package analyzer` and `import (` are visible in the file header, so it is a suitable initial navigation point for the join investigation. The path itself does not indicate that the default window frame is also handled here. Subsequent searches retain this earlier entry point, but no longer let the filename answer for both phenomena.

## First Check What You Have

| Fragment at hand | Retain first | Where to stop |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Join condition | Left and right operands, comparison operator, original location | Only a rewritten expression or `equality lookup` |
| `analyzed plan` or candidate | Place alongside the original condition, retaining references | The condition and plan are not from the same observation |
| job, submission, actual artifact name | Align with a single automated run | The artifact cannot distinguish between conditions |
| window aggregate, frame, state | Whether it is the default, the stage at which the abnormality appears | Only "abnormal after processing" |
| `Empty-OVER child reconstruction` | Record the reconstruction track separately | Do not use it to explain the default frame |

This table sorts the evidence at hand; it does not fill gaps with conclusions. Without the original condition, do not infer direction from the plan; without knowing whether it is the default, do not infer window semantics from the term `frame boundary`; when there is only an adjacent reconstructed object, do not relabel it as the current issue.

```text
An inequality difference in a join or an abnormal state after window processing
├─ Has an original join condition
│  ├─ Preserve the left and right sides and the comparison operator
│  ├─ Follow sql/analyzer/indexed_joins.go to search references
│  ├─ Can connect to the analyzed plan or the same run → continue
│  └─ Only an equality lookup, rewritten form, or isolated path → stop at the join branch
├─ Has no original join condition
│  └─ Record only the labels and paths already seen; do not attribute merge-join
└─ Has a window-state observation
   ├─ Default frame relationship is clear → record the state stage
   ├─ Points to Empty-OVER child reconstruction → split out a reconstruction branch
   └─ Whether it is the default or the module entry is unclear → stop at the window branch
```

The tree's entry point is evidence, not a filename. The two branches may come from the same regression material, but each must independently satisfy the minimum conditions; when only two labels remain, keep both branches pending investigation.

## Join branch: preserve the left and right sides first

First capture the original join condition, rather than the expression later made easier to read. At minimum, retain the left and right operands, the comparison operator, and the context in which it is called an inequality. If you see the left and right sides swapped, the operator rewritten, or bounds reordered, save the "original condition" and the "subsequent form" side by side. Without continuous references, these are just two representations and must not be directly written as an orientation change.

`sql/analyzer/indexed_joins.go` provides only one navigation point for the join branch. `package analyzer` and the file header's `import (` can help confirm that the lookup lands in this local analyzer area, but cannot prove which filters, columns, or expressions have already been consumed here. If following references only reaches an ordinary index, `equality lookup`, or a scalar lookup, record the name and stop. When you see `range collection`, `predicate implication`, `filter pushdown`, or `join lookup`, also ask whether they have a continuous relationship with the original condition; similar terminology does not mean adjacent calls.

When tracing a path, record file-header facts, reference direction, and runtime artifacts separately. The first two come from the source, while the latter comes from the automation entry point; seeing `package analyzer` or `import (` can fill only the first field. Old references also remind us that the actual relationship must be traced back to the references in the specified revision; path similarity cannot substitute for this. This is the search order for the join branch, not a window conclusion.

When narrowing the scope within the local text of that file, first look for join, merge, and index, then check whether equality, scalar, filters, range, column, expressions, bounds, field, and side co-occur; these words only help with filtering, and a single matching word must not be treated as a call edge.

`analyzed plan` is used for comparison with the original condition, not to answer in place of the original condition. When the plan contains only candidate names, write "candidate seen"; when only rewritten bounds are available, write "original condition missing". If the condition, reference, and plan come from different observations, the three cannot be stitched into a single chain. Even if a candidate looks like a suitable index, that does not establish which side the inequality retained.

The observation recorded when GMS-208 were created was "locating the version where Merge-join inequality first changed". The action recorded in the card is to trigger the corresponding job through an existing automation entry point in the repository and record the job, commit, and actual artifact name. The trigger action itself does not answer the direction question: first check whether the artifact can identify the left and right sides and the comparison operator. If a job includes multiple conditions and the artifact does not distinguish them individually, this run can be recorded, but a particular candidate cannot be assigned to this join track; if the artifact name is missing, even the run association is incomplete.

There is a failure loop that has already been followed here: on seeing an index lookup, using the result of `equality lookup` to explain the inequality; on seeing a plan rewrite, treating the rewritten expression as the original condition. Both approaches bypass the continuous chain of references from the input to the consumption point. When recovering, do not rewrite the condition again; return to the last point where the left and right sides can still be identified, and mark whether the original condition, reference, or actual artifact is missing. If only paths and names remain, stop at the join track.

## Window track: first confirm "default"

The window branch first asks whether the observation really involves the default frame. A frame that is not explicitly specified counts only as a candidate; only when default processing can be shown to have occurred does it enter the classification in default-frame. Then record the stage at which the state appears abnormal: when the window definition is formed, when the aggregate is associated, or around subsequent expression reconstruction. If the material contains no stage information, retain only "abnormal state after processing", without supplying a call sequence.

The symptom recorded by GMS-225 is "abnormal state after Window aggregate default processing". The card requires the maintainer of the corresponding module to verify the current behavior and identify an entry point for further inspection. The entry-point request and behavior verification must not be combined: obtaining an entry point does not mean the default frame has been explained; seeing the implementation of an existing branch does not mean the abnormal state has been reproduced. If no module entry point is available, do not copy the join path to fill the gap.

`frame boundary`, window definition, and `expression reconstruction` can only help with classification; the names themselves do not constitute an execution relationship. When you see `expression reconstruction`, first confirm whether it appears in the same observation as the default processing; if they are merely adjacent terms, record its position separately. If the only concrete clue is `Empty-OVER child reconstruction`, go to the adjacent records for DOC-22, indicating that this is a child-node reconstruction clue, not confirmation of the default frame. Even if both names appear in the same material, do not infer the aggregate's expected behavior from the reconstructed object.

The window line also has an easy-to-take-wrong loop: reading "after processing" directly as "after default processing." Fallback does only three things——mark whether the frame was provided explicitly, retain the status text, and request the module entry point. If the first item is unclear, the second can still be retained, but the status cannot be attributed to default-frame; when the entry point is empty, retain the issue rather than substituting the plan, index, or direction from the connection branch.

## Automated runs and existing branches each tell only one part

The connection line must correspond to the previous automated observation that can trace back to the original conditions. The window line currently has a behavior-verification request, a module-entry request, and the review context that "the implementation has been completed in an existing branch." These two types of evidence cannot be interchanged:

| Material scenario | What can be confirmed | What cannot be inferred directly |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Jobs, commits, and artifacts at the automated entry point | A particular job can be traced; if the conditions can be distinguished, the direction can continue to be checked | The window's default frame, or the merge-join direction when conditions are missing |
| Implementation and review on an existing branch | An implementation is available for review, and the review can happen early | That the current window status has been verified, or that a corresponding connection artifact already exists |
| Plan fragment plus source path | The candidate and navigation point are visible | Which side of the inequality the candidate saved |
| Window status text | A rough clue about the anomalous stage remains | That the anomaly necessarily came from the default frame or child-node reconstruction |

The distinction here is not an assessment of implementation quality, but the evidence boundary when writing back. If the same material later contains connection conditions, an explicit marker for the default frame, and a shared module entry point, still retain the two original lines first, then record their intersection separately; until all three appear simultaneously, do not write a common cause.

The automated entry point provides a traceable run, while the existing branch provides a reviewable implementation; missing artifacts from the former do not mean that the latter has no implementation, and an implementation in the latter does not mean that the former has been verified.

## Early entry points and later-narrowed judgments

> Old judgment (retain): Both labels should first be checked starting from `sql/analyzer/indexed_joins.go`; if no common call site is found, initially treat them as the same round of optimizer issue and continue waiting for clues.

This sentence explains why the early records grouped the two signals together. The issue name and call name can indeed lead the initial search to this path, so its navigational value is retained. What could be confirmed later was narrower: the join track can trace condition references from here; the window track must first obtain the default frame and the module entry point. This does not classify the join path as irrelevant, nor does it designate another fixed file for the window track.

The two early substitute actions are also retained: using a normal equality lookup instead of an inequality, or using the implementation status on an existing branch instead of checking window behavior. The former lacks the comparison direction; the latter lacks the correspondence between the status and the default frame. They make the record appear to advance without actually bridging the gap. When taking over, return to the gap rather than continuing to add notes based on the substitutes.

## Constraints left by the card timelines

- Follow-up on the join card began at 2025-10-02 10:40, and it was submitted for review at 14:40. What this leaves for this page is a run-record requirement: the job, commit, and actual artifact name must still be matchable; it did not produce a conclusion about direction.
- Options were compared for the window card at 2025-10-27 11:48, and it was submitted directly for review at 2025-10-28 18:48 because the implementation had already been completed on an existing branch. This action shows that review can precede completion of the behavior check; it does not show that the semantics of the default frame or the stage at which the exception occurs have been proven.
- The two timelines provide no shared execution record. They can be listed side by side in the same closure effort, but cannot substantiate each other: a join job alone still cannot close the window issue, and a window review alone cannot fill in the join direction either.

## When the two tracks can be placed side by side

Mark an intersection in the record only when the same set of material fills the gaps on both tracks. The join side needs the original left and right sides, an unbroken chain of references, and the same job, commit, and actual artifact name; the window side needs how the default frame appears, the state stage, and the module entry point. A shared filename or shared module term is not enough.

If the join run is obtained first, write the join section first, then append the window text that arrives later as a separate paragraph; the reverse works the same way. Do not use later material to backfill earlier judgments. When `Empty-OVER child reconstruction` appears, retain the child-node reconstruction track beside the intersection; it cannot be used in place of the window conditions.

## Writing the gaps back into the record

When the original condition is missing, retain both labels, the path, and any plan terms already seen, explicitly note the input gap, and do not backfill a candidate as the condition. When there is only a job or commit but no actual artifact name, retain the run clues and leave the artifact gap separate; a review of an existing branch cannot substitute for it. When a window has state text but no indication of whether it is the default, record the state and phase, explicitly say if the phase is unknown, and list the module entry-point request separately; if the object is actually `Empty-OVER child reconstruction`, keep it under the adjacent reconstruction track. The three gaps belong to input, run association, and window classification respectively; filling in an item advances only its corresponding branch.

## On-call writeback

When you receive a piece of log, plan, or card text, first label it as one of "condition", "candidate", "run marker", or "window state". Do not combine the four categories into one just because the same passage contains merge, window, or analyzer. Preserve the findings using the following minimal format:

- Condition only: record the left and right sides and the comparison operator, and note that the consumption point has not yet been found.
- Candidate or bounds only: record the observed plan shape, and note that the original condition is missing.
- A job exists but there is no actual artifact name: record the job clues, and retain the artifact gap.
- Window state exists but there is no indication of whether it is the default: record that the post-processing state is abnormal, and leave the frame classification undetermined.
- `Empty-OVER child reconstruction` exists: record the adjacent reconstruction track separately, and do not put it back into the default frame row.

If someone rewrites a condition into a more readable form during review, retain both the original and rewritten text; the recovery action is to add references, not overwrite either version. If all you hear is "the implementation is already on a branch", retain the context of that statement, but stop at behavior not yet checked. This leaves gaps, but does not use similar objects to fabricate an execution chain that does not exist.

## Stop where the evidence supports an explanation

Write back the join track as "original condition → visible reference → plan or run". If an item is missing, identify it: when the same job contains multiple conditions that cannot be distinguished, record only that the run remains unresolved, without specifying a candidate; when there is only a path, record only a navigation point.

Write back the window track as "whether the frame is the default → state phase → module entry point". If default status is unclear, stop at classification; if the phase is unclear, stop at a coarse-grained observation; if the clue turns into `Empty-OVER child reconstruction`, retain navigation to the adjacent record separately. Write the relationship between the two branches together only when the actual material provides an intersection.

```text
Join track: original condition
  ├─ Continuous references + a matching run → proceed to direction review
  ├─ References exist, no matching run → stop at run association
  └─ No original condition → stop at input recovery
Window track: post-processing state
  ├─ Explicitly the default frame + phase → proceed to behavior checking
  ├─ Only state or only the word frame → stop at classification
  └─ Points to Empty-OVER child reconstruction → split off an adjacent track
```

The three questions that still need to be retained are: whether changes to `Merge-join inequality` can be aligned with the same job, commit, and actual artifacts; whether the current window behavior actually goes through the default frame, and at which stage the exception occurs; and whether the window entry point identified by the maintainer intersects with the adjacent rebuild path. These three points concern run correlation, window semantics, and object boundaries, respectively. Without new material, the tree ends here; do not expand a single optimizer exception into a global attribution.

# Generic Equality Lookup Extraction Proposal

For this interface discussion, focus only on Generic equality lookup extraction. The working assumption is that if ordinary equality conditions can be identified reliably, they can become candidate inputs for join lookup; the name alone cannot determine whether they should go through the lookup path.

The earlier investigation notes identify `sql/analyzer/indexed_joins.go` as the starting point for a follow-up check. At the top of the file, we can see `package analyzer` and the import section. This is enough to start checking, but it does not establish that ordinary equality conditions already enter lookup, much less which conditions should be handled here.

There are two approaches to compare. One leaves the interface unchanged and only adds checks on the entry point for ordinary equality conditions; the other lets them become candidates first, then decides whether to use them for lookup. The first requires fewer changes, but the extraction boundary remains unclear. The second focuses the discussion on a single entry point, but we cannot treat every equality as usable.

Both approaches must retain the same question: are the candidates identified the same as the candidates actually used? Without that distinction, we cannot explain the subsequent results.

This draft only discusses the interface. It does not treat a file path or a single static reading as evidence of runtime behavior. What we need to answer is where candidates first appear, and at which step they are ultimately used or dropped.

Find a counterexample first: a condition that looks like an ordinary equality but should not change the join's lookup choice. Do not settle the interface before we have one. # Generic Equality Lookup Extraction Proposal

The initial draft recorded Generic equality lookup extraction as an interface issue and did not treat `sql/analyzer/indexed_joins.go` as a list of changes. The old investigation notes placed the starting point for follow-up checks in this file; `package analyzer` and the import section are visible at the start of the file. This information only indicates where to continue looking; it cannot connect ordinary equality conditions to the final join lookup. The original assumption remains: ordinary equality conditions that are reliably recognized can become candidates; "equality is present" does not mean "already usable for lookup".

## First separate the three states

This trial needs to avoid collapsing three states into a single statement: whether an ordinary equality condition is recognized, whether it is passed to the candidate entry point, and whether a lookup is actually formed during the run. These can differ. Reaching the entry point does not mean that lookup has taken effect; a candidate not being selected does not necessarily imply that it was not extracted. If the record contains only "success" or "failure", there is no way to determine whether to tighten the boundaries of ordinary equality conditions, modify the interface, or continue checking the execution path.

GMS-212 were later linked to a support case, so verification was grounded in an actual CI run: confirm whether Generic equality lookup extraction takes effect, rather than using the existence of a configuration file as a substitute for runtime results. The card provides the entry point for this verification; it does not specify here which ordinary equality conditions should be accepted, nor does it conclude that a particular run has already produced a lookup. This page therefore still describes this as a trial, not as established behavior.

## Proposed narrow entry point

The recommendation is to first let ordinary equality conditions enter the extraction interface as candidates, leaving the final lookup selection to subsequent decisions. Here, generic only means that the entry point is not bound to a special case in advance; it does not mean that all equality conditions have the same eligibility for lookup. The extraction point does not commit to selection in advance, and subsequent decisions do not erase unselected candidates by labeling them "not extracted". This allows counterexamples to fall into two different categories: either the ordinary equality condition should never become a candidate, or it can become a candidate but this run should not use lookup.

This entry point deliberately does not promise a complete list of acceptable forms. The minimum scope of ordinary equality conditions has not yet been defined; there is currently no material supporting a broader definition. `indexed_joins.go` remains the entry point for follow-up checks and does not require the final selection to be made directly at the location indicated by the file path. The cost is retaining one additional intermediate state; the benefit is being able to explain the interface's candidate boundaries separately from runtime selection.

While the scope remains undefined, do not mix different forms in a single trial. First compare the candidate status and runtime outcome for one clearly defined ordinary equality condition; propose expanding the scope only once that comparison can be explained.

The narrow entry point also limits migration costs: before runtime records are obtained, it does not require any existing lookup decision to change its result merely because a candidate is present. Candidates exist only as additional information. If the decision order must later change or the interface scope must expand, that should be a separate decision, not something bundled into this trial.

## Options for discussion

Continuing only to verify the source-code entry point is the most conservative option. It introduces no new candidate semantics, but "whether it takes effect" will still depend on ad hoc judgment. Another option is to assert directly at the extraction point that lookup is available; this appears to remove a step, but actually combines candidate recognition and runtime selection into a single decision, leaving no clear point to modify when a counterexample appears.

This proposal recommends a narrow entry point between these two options, and only as a trial. The trial succeeds if, within the same actual CI run, it is possible to compare the ordinary equality condition under review, whether it became a candidate, and whether that run actually produced a lookup. If the intermediate state is not recorded, state only the observable runtime result without speculating about the extraction step; in that case, this cannot serve as a basis for expanding the interface.

## How to read CI records

The trial does not need to combine a group of similar conditions into a single conclusion. For each verification, first fix the ordinary equality condition being discussed, then record two determinations within the same CI run: whether it reached the candidate entry point, and whether lookup actually took effect. The relationship between the two can only be discussed when both are present; when only the latter is present, the record can only describe the result of that run; when only the former is present, it can only indicate that the extraction interface was reached. This avoids filling in missing intermediate information as causality.

This also changes the meaning of "first find a counterexample" in the initial draft. A counterexample does not have to prove from the outset that the interface is wrong. A condition becoming a candidate without forming a lookup is, first of all, a phenomenon that needs classification; a condition not becoming a candidate only indicates that the boundaries of ordinary equality conditions have not yet been clearly documented. There is reason to return to the interface itself only when the two determinations are seen to contradict each other for the same object in the same run. This sequence makes CI records serve this extraction trial, rather than generalizing a single run into a conclusion about all equality conditions.

## What generic means

Here, generic is the name of the candidate entry point, not an external commitment or shorthand for every future form of equality. If the trial only shows that a certain class of ordinary equality conditions can be recognized, the record should continue to use that narrower description; unchecked forms cannot be included in the scope simply because the interface name contains generic. This restriction prevents a local determination from being incorrectly recorded as a universal rule.

The initial draft presented "do not change the interface" and "expand extraction" side by side. The former is now retained as the fallback after withdrawal; the latter is split into two approaches: a narrow candidate trial and direct assertion at the extraction point. This way, even if the trial stops, the existing entry-point identification and CI verification remain useful, without having to pretend that a broader overhaul has been completed.

## When to stop the trial

What would be withdrawn is the recommendation to "connect ordinary equality conditions to the generic candidate interface", not the old investigation clues. If an actual CI run cannot distinguish candidate entry from lookup taking effect, the trial has not provided enough material to support an interface decision and should revert to entry-point verification. If the boundaries of ordinary equality conditions must depend on a determination unavailable at the extraction point, that determination should not be forced into the generic entry point either. Another reason to stop is a counterexample showing that treating conditions as candidates would mix conditions that should remain in their original handling into lookup decisions; record the counterexample first, then decide whether to tighten the scope or abandon this interface.

The exceptional-case boundaries of Shared optimizer column sets are retained separately in DOC-26. This trial does not incorporate column-set sharing issues into the definition of ordinary equality conditions, nor does it use the conclusions there as a substitute for verification of this run. Still undecided are the minimum scope of ordinary equality conditions, where candidate status should be recorded, and whether the results provided by an actual CI run are sufficient to move subsequent interface decisions forward. Until the records are complete, the proposal remains a narrow-scope trial.

# Troubleshooting Shared Column Set Anomalies

This old on-call page comes from the wrap-up phase of 0.19. The initial signal was that the reported case linked inconsistent results with `Shared optimizer column sets`. Earlier records pointed from the issue name and call name all the way to `sql/analyzer/costed_index_scan.go`, so that file became the first stop. Later addenda retained a narrower assessment: similar names, call names, and paths do not show that the actual call reached that file, much less that this is where the fix belongs.

The old sequence was not deleted so that whoever takes over will first clarify what "shared" means. It might mean a suspicion that the same column set was used repeatedly, or it might only mean that two observations both mentioned columns. The former requires, at a minimum, keeping the same input, entry point, runtime version, and results together; the latter is still only a textual similarity and does not support starting to attribute a cause.

## Preserve the Reported Case First

Keep the input that triggered the difference, the results seen at the time, the version actually running, and the entry point before entering the optimizer in the same record. Then add a separate sentence: does "shared" in the report refer to the same set, the same column name, or the same description? These statements are not interchangeable and should not be merged into "shared column set" when adding notes.

If the input cannot be seen again, the version is only a guess, or the entry point is known only through a secondhand account, stop at the collection stage. Do not split the column set first, and do not extract only a passage of plan text. The former changes the original input, and the latter loses the entry point; both prevent later readers from placing the results back in the original context.

## Branches

```text
Inconsistent results, with a shared column set mentioned
|
+-- The input cannot be reliably seen again
|   `-- Keep the original description of the results; do not change the set or label a cause.
|
`-- The input can be seen again
    |
    +-- The version or entry point is undetermined
    |   `-- Fill in these two items first. Results from different versions or entry points cannot be combined in the same comparison.
    |
    `-- The version and entry point are established
        |
        +-- It is not yet possible to verify that the call passes through the old file
        |   `-- Treat the path as a navigation clue and continue looking for local call relationships; do not derive any changes from this point.
        |
        `-- The call relationship can be verified
            |
            +-- Sharing amounts only to matching names or descriptions
            |   `-- Return to identifying the objects; the difference cannot be attributed to set reuse.
            |
            `-- Repeated use of the same column set can be identified
                `-- Hand it to the implementation team for verification, together with the input, version, entry point, and relationship evidence;
                    keep it unconfirmed until local facts or a counterexample that can explain the difference are obtained.
```

"Can be verified" in the tree does not require reconstructing the entire optimizer chain. The minimum fact needed here is simply that there is a verifiable call relationship between the entry point in the reported case and the retained file. Conversely, seeing the `analyzer` package name, a `import (` block, or similar terms elsewhere does not establish this relationship; these can only explain why the old notes led to this file.

## Keep the Two Cases Separate First

When two results need to be compared, write them side by side as two cases, A and B, rather than first calling them "the same issue". First check whether the inputs are the same, then whether the runtime versions and entry points are the same. If the inputs differ, keep each on its own branch; if the inputs are the same but the versions differ, leave the difference in the version dimension for now; if the versions are the same but the entry points differ, leave the difference in the entry-point dimension for now. This separation does not declare which dimension is the cause; it only prevents attributing two changes to the shared column set at the same time.

Only when both A and B can identify repeated use of the same object may "shared" be recorded as a common condition of the two records. If one side provides only a column name while the other refers to a set, first preserve the original meaning of each term. Forcing the terminology to match would mislead later investigators into thinking that the objects have already been matched.

If the new entry-point name differs from the old record, do not immediately classify it as another issue either. First check whether it can be tied to the same input and the same runtime version; if not, retain it as a separate case. A name change alone is not evidence of object identity.

## Use the Old Entry Point Only for Navigation

Only after confirming the prerequisites should you follow `v_prev` in the record to open `sql/analyzer/costed_index_scan.go`. This old entry-point record can confirm only that the file is in the `analyzer` package, along with several local declarations and adjacency clues. A path is not another name for implementation responsibility. In particular, neither the filename nor the directory location justifies inferring that the column set must be created, rewritten, or returned here.

When reading this file, narrow the question to two things: whether the entry point from the reported case exists in that snapshot; and, if it does, whether the relationship between the entry point and this file can be verified directly. If the first question has no answer, do not fill the gap with a later runtime version. If the second relationship breaks, stop at the break rather than filling in intermediate layers with similar names.

Even after the relationship can be verified, what you record should still be local observations. For example, you may write that a suspected column set appears near this part of the relationship; you may not supply it with an unsupported lifecycle. If the reported case can only say "the columns look the same", retain that the column names or descriptions match; only when repeated use of the same object can be identified should "shared set" be retained as the object for the next verification step. Even then, it only makes the suspicion more specific; it does not explain the cause of the difference in results.

## Arrows Left by Earlier Notes

The tentative assessment in the earlier passage was: first assume that the same column set is used repeatedly along the optimizer path, then trace backward from `costed_index_scan.go`. At the time, this assessment was used to reduce the number of directions being investigated at once, not as a confirmed attribution. The original passage is still retained to make it clear why the old path was prioritized.

The original passage also warned against treating temporary splitting or rebuilding of the set as a fix. This stopping point still applies: if the difference disappears after rewriting, that only shows that the input has been manually changed; it cannot be used to infer a sharing relationship. If this has already been tried, record the original input and the rewritten input separately; the latter must not overwrite the former or serve as the sole basis for a change.

Later verification did not provide material that would turn path similarity into implementation ownership. The old arrows can therefore still help locate a starting point for reading, but no longer point to direct changes. What is retained here is the blind spot at the time, not a finalized implementation description.

## Old Notes Retained in the Margin

> Old note: when you see wording about a column set, look at `costed_index_scan.go` first.

This sentence saved a lot of time early on, but it saved navigation time, not confirmation time. The later clarification changed it to "first verify whether the entry point passes through that location". Both sentences are retained together: the first explains why the path appears repeatedly, and the second prevents it from being used to assign implementation ownership. Without an entry-point relationship, the old note can only lead someone to the file; it cannot place the issue in the file.

Another on-call practice has also been retained: if temporarily changing the set changes the results, first record the action alongside the original input, then undo that rewrite. This is not a recovery procedure; its only value is to prevent the behavior after rewriting from overwriting the initial behavior.

## Two Columns for Addenda

The later record first constrained the earlier assessment with a negative condition: two descriptions both mentioning a column set does not mean they come from the same runtime version or the same entry point, or even that they refer to the same object. This condition is enough to reject shortcut attribution; it neither proves that the shared column set is unrelated nor designates another responsible location.

| Already retained | Still to be established |
| --- | --- |
| Original descriptions of the input and the results at the time | Whether the same difference can occur again with that input |
| Explicitly stated runtime version | Whether that version was the one actually running in the reported case |
| Reported entry point | Whether the entry point can be connected to the old file |
| The wording about "sharing" | Whether the same column set was used repeatedly |

When an item is missing from the left column, speculation cannot fill in the right column. The table only separates facts from items still to be checked; it does not elevate a vague line of description into a completed reproduction.

## Before Handoff

The material handed to the implementation team should be a set of items that can all be placed back in the same case: the original input and results, the actual version, the entry point, and the local relationship from the entry point to the old file. If these four items are scattered across different records, whoever takes over can only guess again at what "shared" means. If the relationship has not yet been found, the handoff should state that the path is only for navigation, not claim that the issue has already been located in that file.

When handing off to the quality team, the focus is whether the original behavior can be seen again. Failure to see it again does not mean the report is wrong; it only means this record cannot yet be used to determine whether a regression exists. Do not replace the original results with results obtained after splitting the set, and do not merge two entry points into a single sample merely because column names appear at both.

If the implementation team provides a counterexample, use it to change the current branch first rather than reinforcing the earlier assumption. If the entry point does not pass through the old file, or the supposed sharing does not involve the same object, the investigation returns to object identification or call relationships; there is no need to expand the scope to the entire optimizer.

## Reopening a Stopped Record

For a record that has already stopped, do not resume guessing from the furthest path reached last time. First place new material into its corresponding gap: input, runtime version, entry point, call relationship, or object identification. Fill in only the level it can support. For example, a newly obtained version can only resolve the undetermined version; it cannot also prove that the entry point passes through the old file.

If new material only corrects the meaning of "shared", return to object identification; if it provides only a path, remain at the navigation level. Keep the original record alongside it rather than overwriting the old wording with new phrasing. This lets whoever takes over see which gap has been filled and which questions remain unanswered.

If added material conflicts with the old description, first write out the conflict side by side rather than silently replacing the old sentence. The most common conflicts here concern not the conclusion but differences in the object referred to by "shared", the entry point in the reported case, or the runtime version. The next step in the tree is meaningful only after the conflict has been separated out.

If the new material is only a file excerpt, it adds only observations near the path. It cannot replace the input and results from the reported case, much less the relationship from the entry point to the file.

In new records, write the original terms first and the interpretation afterward; do not backfill the interpretation into the old case. This preserves the earlier ambiguity of the word "shared".

## Stopping Points

Stop in four situations: there is no input available for comparison; there is no actual runtime version; the entry point and file are connected only by name; or the only "improvement" comes from manually changing the set. For the first two, fill in the case details first; for the third, fill in the relationship first; for the fourth, restore the original input before looking again. These are not the same failure and should not be closed out with the same conclusion.

One to-do remains at the bottom of the page: when the next case arrives, first add an original record that brings the entry point, version, and results together, then decide whether it is worth continuing along the old path. Until then, this page provides only the old entry point and stopping points; it cannot declare a cause on behalf of the reported case.

# Top-N row-shape decision record

Following the old investigation leads left in `v_prev`, both the issue name and the call name initially point to `sql/rowexec/join_iters.go`. Treat the row shape of Top-N as a local issue on the rowexec side to start with: first check whether rows handed off by the join iterator can still be read using their original column positions, then discuss the sorting side. This order only narrows the scope of the initial inspection; a path name is not a complete call relationship.

Row shape here does not mean the number of results, nor does it mean only the sort condition. It means that after a row object is selected into the top N, downstream code can still interpret its column positions and expressions as the same content. If the order is correct but the interpretation on read has changed, that cannot be recorded merely as a sorting discrepancy; conversely, selecting the wrong top N does not automatically make it a row-shape issue.

There were three options on the table at the time: preserve the interpretation of the row on the join iterator side; have the row sorter hold both the sorting logic and the row interpretation; or have the Top-N heap restore column positions when storing candidates. The decision was to use the first option. The available leads pointed only to `join_iters.go`; the other two options would bring candidates, sort conditions, and expression handling into the change together, making the scope too broad.

On that basis, Top-N will not introduce a separate row container, the row sorter will not add expression reconstruction, and the Top-N heap will not be responsible for column positions. If we later see that the same row cannot be read using the same column positions before and after selection, revisit this decision. The handling point remains the join iterator for the time being.

# Top-N Row Shape Decision Record

The old memo had a very narrow focus: first examine the row shape of Top-N on the rowexec side, specifically by opening `sql/rowexec/join_iters.go`. The initial investigation was led to this file by the issue name and call name, rather than starting from an execution path that had already been traced end to end. The initial draft therefore described it as the point to address and placed `row sorter` and `Top-N heap` on the side to leave untouched for now.

This wording saved discussion at the time. It narrowed the broad question of "where Top-N might change rows" to one place to examine first, and avoided changing sort conditions, candidates, and expressions all at once from the outset. But in subsequent retellings, "look here first" could easily become "only this needs to change." This addendum retains the old choice and simply states the assumptions it depends on alongside it.

## The Decision Recorded at the Time

> For Top-N, do not create a separate row carrier. The join iterator preserves the interpretation of rows; the row sorter handles sorting only, and the Top-N heap only retains candidates. If column positions or expressions in a row deviate, address the issue on the join iterator side first.

This passage was the initial draft's decision, not a rule formulated later. It understood Top-N row-shape integrity to mean that after a row enters the selection of the first N items, downstream code can still interpret that row using its original column positions and expressions. It does not refer to the number of results, nor does it treat the sort condition itself as the row shape. Correct ordering of the first N candidates does not, by itself, show that the reader sees the original kind of row; incorrect sorting also does not automatically mean that the row object has been rewritten.

The initial draft did not separate "which candidates to select" from "reading the retained objects" as two questions. The former concerns ordering and truncation; the latter concerns column positions, expressions, and which interpretation is still used when reading. The old position assumed that there was no intervening handoff that needed to be identified separately: the join iterator produces rows, the selection process retains only some of them, and the reader continues to retrieve values as before. This assumption made a local change look minimal, while also overstating the boundaries of responsibility.

## The Three Locations on the Table

What was compared at the time was not three verified call chains, but three ways to place the responsibility for protection. Each approach answered the same narrow question: if a selected row can no longer be read using the old column positions, which object should first be required to preserve that correspondence. The initial draft described the other two options very briefly; they are filled in below so that "not adopted" is not misread as "irrelevant."

**A: join iterator.** This was the position actually adopted. It assumes that rows entering the selection process already carry stable column positions and expression interpretations; as long as the join iterator does not break that interpretation when handing over a row, subsequent selection should not have to repair it. The existing investigation pointed only to `join_iters.go`, so this also appeared to be the least costly place to address the issue: there was no need to create a new row wrapper for Top-N, or to broaden the meaning of the row sorter.

The cost of this choice was not stated in the initial draft. If the row's form has already been converted before or after sorting, or if a candidate does not hold the object that downstream code reads directly, the join iterator cannot preserve the row shape even if it remains unchanged. Placing the fix there could also obscure the actual handoff point. Nevertheless, the decision at the time was to proceed with A first, because no material indicated that the other two locations had to be involved.

**B: row sorter.** The second position places responsibility closer to the sorting handoff: after comparing the sort condition, if the row sorter hands over a different row form, that is where the continuing correspondence of column positions and expressions should be specified. The initial draft did not adopt this option. This was not because it had been confirmed that the row sorter was absent from the relevant path, but because of concern about tying "determining sort order" and "maintaining the interpretation of result rows" to one object. If it is responsible only for comparison, adding expression reconstruction would expand its responsibilities; if it already holds that interpretation, then A in the initial draft is missing another assumption.

B was therefore deferred, not disproved. At the time, the old memo was more concerned with reducing the scope of changes: let the sorting side focus only on sorting, and keep row interpretation upstream. This distinction is clean in design terms, but requires an unstated condition—the sorting side must indeed not reorganize, project, or wrap rows that will later be read. Without that condition, "the row sorter is not responsible" is only a preference, not a conclusion.

**C: Top-N heap.** The third position places the issue where candidates are retained. It treats the heap as the object that may be closest to "retaining the first N items": if candidates no longer have their original row form when entering or leaving the heap, the heap at least needs to know what downstream code can read. The initial draft did not adopt C because it treated the heap as a temporary storage detail during selection, believing that it only needed to preserve candidate order and should not know about column positions or expressions.

C's implicit cost is the opposite of A's. If the heap is required to carry row shape, its interface may no longer be merely a candidate container; if the heap actually stores only original rows, adding restoration logic would create an extra conversion layer out of nothing. The old record did not confirm what it stores, so "the heap is irrelevant" cannot be inferred from the filename or object name. Even so, the initial draft excluded it from the scope of changes, which was an explicit earlier decision.

The initial draft compared compatibility costs only in terms of change scope: putting the responsibility in the row sorter would bring row interpretation into the sorting side; putting it in the Top-N heap would change the responsibility for retaining candidates; leaving it in the join iterator would bet on it already having crossed the relevant handoff. A was chosen because it appeared to affect the least at the time, not because the three costs had already been measured.

expression reconstruction was brought into the discussion because unchanged column positions and unchanged expression interpretations are not always the same thing. An object can retain its original column positions while presenting the reader with different expressions; it can also reconstruct expressions and ultimately still produce a row that can be read using the old column positions. The initial draft assigned both cases to the join iterator to keep the judgment in one place, not because they were known to always occur at the same implementation layer.

To prevent later readers from interpreting the three placement options as a call chain, the record retains them as choice states. The arrows in the diagram indicate only review outcomes, not data flowing from one object to another.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    state "Placement options under review" as Review
    state "join iterator" as JoinIterator
    state "row sorter" as RowSorter
    state "Top-N heap" as TopNHeap
    [*] --> Review
    Review --> JoinIterator: Adopted in the initial draft
    Review --> RowSorter: Deferred
    Review --> TopNHeap: Deferred
    JoinIterator --> [*]
    RowSorter --> [*]
    TopNHeap --> [*]
```

## Brief Notes from the Path Recheck

The recheck returned to `v_prev` in `internal/GMS`, and the file opened was still `sql/rowexec/join_iters.go`. What can be seen directly from this local material is `package rowexec` and `import (` in the file header. This is enough to show that the old entry point did not identify the wrong file, but it cannot automatically connect the issue name, the call name, and the actual runtime relationship of Top-N. Neither rowexec in the directory nor join in the filename is, by itself, an assignment of responsibility.

This weakens only one word in the initial draft: `join_iters.go` can remain the first file to open, but can no longer be described as the only implementation point that needs to be examined. The recheck did not obtain a reference sufficient to transfer responsibility to the row sorter or the Top-N heap, nor did it obtain a runtime example that could completely overturn A. The addendum therefore does not establish a new focal point; it preserves the order of investigation in the old decision while withdrawing its claim of exclusivity.

The initial draft also turned "address it on the join iterator side first" into "complete it on the join iterator side." The former is an investigation order, while the latter assigns implementation responsibility; without reference relationships, the two cannot be used interchangeably. The addendum withdraws only the latter statement, while the former remains in the old decision.

Here, "where the shape becomes visible" must be distinguished from "who maintains the shape." The former may become apparent only when downstream code reads by column position or expression; the latter may occur at an earlier handoff. By placing both questions on the join iterator, the initial draft misread "column positions were not changed here" as "the selection process will not change the row shape." That inference is not supported on this page, but its opposite has not been proved either.

A counterexample that could genuinely undermine A should be very narrow: the order of the selected first N items remains acceptable, but when downstream code reads the same candidate, its column positions or expression interpretation cannot be preserved. Such a case separates sorting errors from row shape errors, making it worth reopening the discussion of placement. If the order itself is also wrong, or if what is retrieved is not even the same candidate, all three objects could be implicated, and responsibility cannot be assigned solely from a mixed symptom. This page does not present such a counterexample as an incident that has already occurred.

The absence of obvious changes in the join iterator cannot prove A; it still does not answer what the objects are before selection, during selection, and when downstream code reads them.

## The Position That Was Not Rewritten

Even with these gaps left by the path recheck, the old memo retains an operational decision: first understand row interpretation on the join iterator side, do not introduce a separate set of row carriers for Top-N, and do not put expression reconstruction directly into the row sorter. The reason for this decision remains the assessment of change scope made at the time, not a complete description of the actual implementation. It is suitable for explaining why the initial draft did not change all three locations at once, but not for treating it as a general assignment of responsibility for other paths.

For B, the old decision still holds that sort conditions and result row interpretation should not be combined unnecessarily. For C, the old decision still holds that the heap should not take on column-position restoration because of a symptom whose components have not been separated. Neither statement has gained new empirical support in the current record; they are retained so that later readers can see why expansion was rejected at the time, rather than replacing them with equally arbitrary opposite conclusions.

Therefore, this review did not approve transferring responsibility to the row sorter, nor did it approve adding a restoration layer to the heap. If someone reopens this page because of the row shape of Top-N, the old order is still to examine `join_iters.go` first; that order simply can no longer be used to infer that the change must be made in that file. This distinction may look small, but it is the boundary missing from the initial draft.

## The Links Still to Be Established

- Whether the object handed over by the join iterator and the object received by the selection stage have the same row form.
- Whether the row sorter only compares the sort condition on the relevant path, or also hands over objects for downstream code to read.
- Whether the Top-N heap retains original rows, candidates, or another intermediate form.
- The earliest point at which downstream code interprets selected rows by column position or expression.
- If conversions exist between the three locations, who should preserve the correspondence before and after each conversion.

These questions have not been made into new acceptance criteria. They are simply gaps the old decision did not answer. Leaving them here is more consistent with the conclusions this record could support at the time than changing A to "confirmed," or B and C to "actually responsible."

Finally, one easily overlooked limitation remains: the location of `sql/rowexec/join_iters.go` is the old investigation entry point, not an explanation of the naming of Top-N. The path is still worth reading from the beginning because it was the foothold left at the time; but the local file header in rowexec cannot substitute for reference relationships. The old conclusion has therefore not been deleted and should only be used within its original narrow scope.

# Schema-Qualified Statistics Plan

This review initially treated Schema-qualified statistics as a minor interface-tightening change, assuming that adding a schema to the statistics lookup would prevent qualification information from being lost in the call chain. This wording remained in the initial draft; it later had to be revised. The initial draft starts its lookup from `sql/analyzer/catalog.go`, while the file itself only shows `package analyzer` and the immediately following `import (`. These fragments only show that the record was once looked up from the analyzer side; they do not show that catalog constructed the statistics key.

> Retained initial-draft tendency: complete the schema on the catalog side while keeping the provider's old input.
>
> What appealed at the time was the smaller call surface; the initial draft did not answer where the default schema comes from or where unqualified input goes.

The second version has withdrawn the claim that "catalog is the owner" and links GMS-217 to this discussion. The card's instructions require adding the Schema-qualified statistics example from the user's report to the repository tests, while retaining the current failure text or output bytes. The instructions do not clearly identify the failure stage: they do not distinguish identity propagation, the statistics lookup, cost selection, or some other downstream stage. Therefore, this example cannot establish what identity the provider has received, nor can an output change be interpreted in advance as the result of cost selection.

The card only constrains how the example is retained; it does not specify the interface shape. Treating it as authorization for an interface change would repeat the initial draft's mistake of treating navigation material as an ownership conclusion.

What is retained this time is not a complete migration plan, but an abortable trial. First prepare a pair of inputs that differ only in whether they are schema-qualified: one explicitly includes a schema, while the other retains the old unqualified form. Keep the observation points only near the statistics query boundary: the table identity before entry, the visible output after entry, and the failure text or output bytes. The comparison here is not whether the two cases produce the same output, but whether the qualification information is still present when it reaches the boundary; if the unqualified input originally depends on the default schema, that dependency should be written down rather than silently filled in by the test.

The trial is deliberately limited to the interface and the examples. It does not require changing the statistics record format, nor does it directly record any particular output difference as evidence of cost selection. The example must retain the schema spelling in the input; if output is retained, keep only the failure text or output bytes, rather than replacing it with a sentence saying "still fails." This makes it possible during later review to distinguish checking identity propagation from guessing about downstream behavior.

There are still two candidate interfaces, with different costs.

**A — Normalize within the analyzer.** Callers can still submit a table name, and the analyzer adds the schema before passing it downstream. This looks closest to the first draft, but the default choice would remain in the local context. If a caller has already lost a stable schema on entry, this approach merely postpones the guess; it should not be approved on the grounds of "fewer changes."

**B — Carry the full identity in the query interface.** Callers pass in a table identity that includes the schema, and the provider reads statistics using that identity. This direction keeps qualification semantics at the boundary, but each existing caller needs to be checked to see whether it can supply that same identity. Its migration cost has not been fully accounted for on this page, and the catalog path should not be used to endorse it in advance.

Change the verification order to: first check whether the object the caller sends into the analyzer already has a schema, then check whether the provider's actual boundary preserves it. Only when both points can be clearly documented should we compare which layer should change its interface. Inferring callers outward from `catalog.go` risks treating a filename as a contract; DOC-31 can be used to find the integration testing entry point, but cannot replace this check.

Beyond these two approaches, the conservative option proposed in the second version remains valid: leave the provider unchanged for now and only add regression cases. This is not the end state; it simply avoids breaking old inputs while the failure location is unknown. Cases can preserve differences, but cannot replace the interface trade-off.

The decision branches are recorded here so that next time we do not start from the same assumption again:
- If schema qualification has already been erased before reaching the query boundary, prioritize revisiting B, with A as an alternative for deciding whether default completion is allowed.
- If the qualification information is still present but the error occurs after the query, withdraw this interface change; keep the cases, but do not attribute responsibility to the provider.
- If the schema for unqualified inputs can only be guessed from the environment, first decide whether the old semantics must be preserved. Without that decision, neither A nor B can begin migration.

One related issue has not yet been separated out: when an old caller does not include a schema, is the default schema part of the caller's semantics, or a fallback in the query layer? The first draft treated it as an implementation detail; the current draft leaves it as a migration prerequisite. Without this answer, regression cases can only show differences, not determine the interface.

This round corrects an inference; it does not confirm any particular implementation: `sql/analyzer/catalog.go` remains an entry point for verification and is no longer described as the established location for schema normalization. The outstanding questions are also more specific: what the provider actually receives, whether the statistics key and table identity are the same concept, and whether old callers need to supply a schema or are allowed to omit it. If the answer to any of these forces existing unqualified inputs to take a different path, stop the trial at the case level and retain the old interface.

# Postmortem: Object State Discrepancy During Caller Integration Testing

The real call samples left by `client` and `example` are used to confirm the adapter boundary and support integration feedback. Two checks of the same object at the current entry point returned different `current revision`. At the first check, `window definition` at the current entry point also did not match the old record. Both discrepancies arose within the same integration assessment, so we could not treat the state seen later as a natural continuation of the earlier one.

The most tempting initial explanation was that the old record was out of date. Once another `current revision` appeared at the entry point on the second check, that explanation was not enough to reach a conclusion: even if the entry point had simply been updated, we would still need to know when the update happened. What was missing was precisely the point in time between the two states. Nor could this difference in the definition therefore be attributed to `regression selector`; the available records contained no link between the two. An outdated record could not be identified as the cause of this incident.

## Sequence Recorded During the Investigation

1. **First check**: `window definition` at the current entry point differed from the old record. Only the mismatch itself was recorded; its source was not determined.
2. **Second check**: The same entry point showed another `current revision`. This at least establishes that the two states were seen in sequence; it does not establish that they conflicted at the same point in time.
3. **Retries stopped**: Repeatedly reading the current entry point could not recover the intervening window and would instead mix later states into the original incident evidence. We therefore preserved the version from that time and stopped retrying.
4. **Recovery result appeared**: `expression reconstruction` can be recovered. This result was placed on the recovery page alongside the original incident evidence, without replacing the initial failure window.
5. **Review stopping point**: Why `regression selector` changed remained unconfirmed. Branches that had not been reproduced were left as unknown, not treated as recovered.

"Retries stopped" means that subsequent reads of the current entry point were no longer used to overwrite the original incident evidence. It does not mean that the recovery result was deleted. The preserved version from that time is in `docs/adj-sql/incidents/sql-caller-integration-testing-two-states-for-the-same-object.md`; the original record remains here, and the recovery page is retained separately. Continuing to read the entry point could not bring back the missing point in time, which was also why we stopped then.

## The Three Records Were Not Merged

The original record, recovery page, and unconfirmed cause are retained separately; they cannot be collapsed into a single final version. The original record preserves the first observed mismatch between the definition and the entry point state; the recovery page preserves the recovery result for `expression reconstruction`; the unconfirmed cause remains the question of why the current entry point displayed different `current revision` at two points in time. Overwriting the original record with the recovery page would erase the intervening window and the initial failure window, leaving later readers with only a seemingly stable state.

The two revisions at the current entry point cannot, on their own, prove that the entry point itself changed, nor can they prove that the call samples from `client` or `example` have changed. A mismatched definition likewise cannot, on its own, prove that the adapter boundary has changed. The partial result on the recovery page cannot retroactively fill in this interval. We therefore did not record `regression selector` as the cause or use the recovery result to rewrite the old record.

## Impact on Integration Testing

Integration feedback depends on these real call samples. Without a shared point in time for the states, we cannot assess the adapter boundary solely from the revision last displayed at the entry point, nor can we treat the recovery page as evidence that the old samples have been corrected. The related work still has its own schedule, maintainer, and exit criteria; the state discrepancy did not provide a shared point in time that could be used to confirm those exit criteria.

Recovery establishes only that the recovery page recorded that `expression reconstruction` can be recovered. It does not prove that the definition has returned to what the old record showed, nor does it establish when or why `regression selector` changed. Integration feedback can distinguish between the original incident evidence and the recovery result, but neither can replace the other.

This has not changed the purpose of the samples from `client` and `example`. They still support adapter-boundary assessment and integration feedback; the states returned by the same entry point at different times simply cannot be collapsed into a single revision. When citing a sample, indicate whether it comes from the original incident evidence or the recovery result.

## The Missing Interval

What is missing is the record window between the two entry point states. Without intervening records, there is no basis for interpreting the two observations as one continuous change. The available material establishes only that a mismatch was observed, that `expression reconstruction` could later be recovered, and that the cause remained unconfirmed. The available records also provide no grounds for treating either state as a correction of the other. Only by filling in this window can we distinguish an entry point change from an outdated record. Any records obtained must fall between the two observations to have a chance of filling this gap in the assessment. If no records were left for that window, retain "cannot determine"; do not select one `current revision` and backfill it as the sole historical state.

# Client Integration Testing Exit Window Checklist

This checklist preserves the exit-window criteria used on one occasion for sql-client-integration. It checks only the exit action, the last visible result, and the exit action for adj-sql. Whether the release succeeded still requires separate sign-off from the relevant owner; completing this checklist means only that the exit records were written down at the time, not that the release was approved.

The old version used `frame boundary` to locate the captured state, held off on cleanup at `compatibility guard`, and treated the absence of `cumulative upgrade` as a stop point. These terms remain in the record to help trace the sequence of operations at the time. They cannot, on their own, prove that the current entry point has finished running or turn an internal-view result into a user-side result.

The old version also left recovery as an action still to be tried. Recovery has still not been tried in the shared environment; the recovery branch below only specifies when to stop and back out along the recorded sequence. Cleanup must not be documented as a verified step. If the records from that time have already been cleared, note what is missing and stop before recovery. Do not backfill the record with similar results from a new run.

## Capture the Sample

- [ ] Start replay with the original sql-client-integration input. Keep the original input, the revision used, and the first visible result in the same record; do not reconstruct an input that merely looks similar.
- [ ] Look for both the current entry point and the original current revision. If the entry point can be found but the revision cannot, or vice versa, record which one is missing; if neither can be found, leave the status unknown and stop making further judgments.
- [ ] State whether the result came from the internal view or the user-side exit entry point. The internal view establishes only what was visible there; it cannot stand in for a user-side replay.
- [ ] Before starting the exit action, preserve the records around `frame boundary`. This is a locator term from the old checklist, not a pass marker.

Keep the entry point and revision together as a pair in the record. Any output seen later that cannot be linked back to this pair can only be retained as output on its own; it cannot be entered as the replay result for the original input.

## During Exit

The two exit actions cannot substitute for each other. If sql-client-integration has exited while adj-sql is still active, record the former as executed and the latter as incomplete; if the order is reversed, record that as well and keep the window open.

1. First confirm that this exit action has been executed, then confirm that the exit action for adj-sql has also finished. If either side is still changing, preserve the state rather than clearing the other side's records first.
2. Check whether the last visible result still corresponds to the original input and the revision used. If only a new, similar input can be found, stop replay; a similar input cannot replace the original sample.
3. On reaching `compatibility guard`, hold off on cleanup as specified in the old procedure. This point preserves the boundary as it stood at the time; it does not mark the result as "successful."
4. If `cumulative upgrade` has not appeared, mark the window incomplete. If exit has already started and recovery is needed, back out only along the recorded exit steps. Recovery has not been tried in the shared environment; do not expand the scope of operations ad hoc while closing the window.
5. Incomplete items must identify the affected entity and the person taking over. Items without an assigned owner stay on the checklist; other boxes being checked does not make the release complete.

## Restrictions Added Later

Dependency checks, risk review, and user-side replay cannot be combined into a single status. After the dependency checks were completed, reproduction remained blocked because approval for the read-only account was pending; this establishes only that the dependencies were reviewed, not that the user-side entry point was run. Risk review cannot fill this gap either. The record contains only the internal view, and the user-side exit entry point was not run, so that result can serve only as the last result seen in the internal view.

If the account is not ready, leave user-side replay marked as not run. Do not fill it in using another input or the internal view. Do not clean up the preserved state while approval is pending; if an exit action already in progress must be reversed, recover using the recorded steps above. This recovery branch has not been tried in the shared environment. Stop if anything differs rather than guessing the next step within the window.

- [ ] The original input, revision, entry point, and last visible result can all be linked to each other; if the current entry point and original current revision are missing, record the status as unknown.
- [ ] Retain results for both the exit action performed and the exit action for adj-sql; do not change the fact that the user-side run was not performed into a pass.
- [ ] Hand the release decision back to the relevant owner, keeping account approval and incomplete replay with the record.
