# Dependency Boundary Entry Point Migration Index

This index was not deleted along with the old entry point. Some adoption records still refer back from here to integration-supply-boundary: the dependency sources documented around lock and license, along with their respective adoption scopes and exit responsibilities. Early on, "the entry point changed" was written as a single event, but in fact at least three things were happening in parallel: whether the old entry point was still readable, whether content had been written at the replacement location, and whether a particular caller was still reading through the old entry point. When all three have not been confirmed together, the index preserves their statuses side by side and does not state an overall completion conclusion.

The reference point is still `docs/adj-integration/migration/Current entry point-Old entry point migration index.md`. This contains a mixture of early assessments, maintenance locations added later, and callers that have not yet been rechecked. "Current entry point" in the filename was merely the page name originally used to place the new and old entry points side by side; it does not mean every row has switched over. The attachments and body are still maintained by integration · Dependency Boundary Audit; this page keeps the relationships among old paths, new locations, and consumers together.

Each record is separated by source. The lock description and the license description each have their own adoption scope; they must not be collapsed into a single statement that "the dependencies have been handled" just because their names are similar. Exit responsibilities are also preserved with each source: who maintains the old entry point, when it can be removed, and where reads will continue after removal. The independent schedule, maintainer, and exit conditions belong to the same source record; do not casually move them to another record when changing pages.

## The Two Ends of an Index Row

The old entry point is not just a historical link. On this page, it is also a recovery point; the replacement location is where new maintenance text is added; only the third item identifies callers still using it. Leave callers that could not be reached explicitly marked "not rechecked"; do not mark them as migrated just because a new entry point appears in the directory. This may leave old and new text next to each other, but it makes it possible to distinguish a source that still uses the old entry point from one that merely encounters a broken link.

|Location|What should remain|What this must not be taken to mean|
|---|---|---|
|Old entry point|Original assessment, source description, recovery point|All adopters have migrated away|
|Replacement location|New maintenance location and field-level corrections|The old entry point can be removed immediately|
|Caller column|The location actually reached or "not rechecked"|A readable directory means completion|
|Exit responsibility|Conditions for retention, rollback, or handoff|A page rename means ownership has been transferred|

```text
Before migration
Old entry point ──> Dependency source / Adoption record
  │                 └─> Callers still using it
  └─> Location that can be restored

After partial migration
Old entry point ──> Retained as a recovery point
Replacement location ──> New maintenance location
                     └─> Records checked by tracing actual consumers
```

Separate "entry point" from "content" when writing rows. A link opening only means that page is readable; whether the source description has migrated depends on whether the replacement location contains the corresponding text; whether the adoption scope has migrated depends on what actual callers read; exit responsibility requires a separate check for explicit retention or handoff. Do not combine these four assessments. When an old paragraph contains an error, add a correction below it rather than overwriting it with a clean new sentence.

## Leave Batches As They Were

A migration batch is not the final state of an overall table. Each batch records only the dependency sources, old entry points, replacement locations, and verification participants encountered in that batch; if only one consumer was traced this time, do not list other callers of the same source as compatible. Keep old paths, new paths, and compatible callers in their respective places, and do not backfill later results into the previous batch.

Names are the easiest things to conflate across batches. Similar names for two entry points do not mean they represent the same dependency source; two callers reading the same text does not mean their adoption scopes are the same. The index places them side by side only when existing records explicitly connect them; it does not infer relationships from page names, directory levels, or a reply.

Keep two questions at the end of each batch: what this move changed, and what has still not been rechecked. The former may be the replacement location, adoption scope, or exit responsibility; the latter may still be the readability of the old entry point, actual consumers, or a replay of an adjacent boundary. Writing items that have not been rechecked at the end of the batch makes them easier to find during rollback than hiding them in an overall status.

Do not rewrite the original text of early batches because of later confirmations. When a correction appears after the original text, readers should be able to tell whether it concerns the entry point, source description, or caller, rather than assuming the entire record has been replaced. Keeping the old assessment alongside the result for the new maintenance entry point on that occasion was precisely intended to make this kind of local change visible.

Therefore, when a batch only finishes adding the replacement location, the index may still show the old entry point, consumers that have not been rechecked, and unchanged exit responsibilities at the same time. This is not a conflict; it is the boundary left by that batch. If the next batch changes the adjacent integration-supply-boundary, start a separate paragraph for it too, rather than borrowing the previous batch's completion marker.

Do not describe callers absent from a batch as there being no callers. When no one has traced the old entry point, the adoption scope remains unknown; when there are no exit conditions, the old entry point remains an item to retain. This blank is not a formatting omission; it indicates which section should be filled in first the next time the index is opened.

## Tracing One Actual Consumer

Select one actual consumer from the old entry point and follow the path it actually reads to the current revision. This is the verification method left by GMSC-010: stop at the first difference, rather than guessing the rest of the chain as soon as the replacement page is seen. The first difference may be in the entry point, the maintenance location referenced by the record, or the content the caller reads. The index records only the difference actually encountered and preserves the preceding path.

On the first pass, keep the old entry point and caller fixed, write down what it reads first, and then check the replacement location; do not change all three locations at once. If the goal is to confirm whether a caller has really left the old entry point, do not change the adjacent input. If the goal is to see the difference caused by an adjacent boundary, keep the current entry point and original access path unchanged and record caller verification separately. Both operations may produce a "difference," but those differences do not mean the same thing.

When an actual consumer stops at the old entry point, record "stopped at the old entry point"; do not interpret this as the caller not existing. When it reaches the replacement location but still reads the old assessment, the replacement location may only be marked "reached," not "completed." Once it can reach the current revision, move this consumer from the not-rechecked column to the verified column; this entry covers only that consumer and does not vouch for a bypass path with the same name.

In the past, some people organized the directory first and added callers later. This order left entries containing new locations alongside old callers. Now, instead of backfilling early records, add the first difference below the original entry. This way, when looking back at old batches, it is still possible to see whether the entry point actually changed at the time or only the directory changed.

## When Execution Records Point to 404

During the migration cleanup in GMSC-003, the index recorded an observation: when following the execution record, the page corresponding to the current result was already 404. This observation only shows that this access relationship was broken; it must not be described as the dependency source having disappeared, nor can it be used to determine that the old entry point is invalid. The index therefore preserves the point-in-time label of the old assessment and appends maintenance locations that could later be confirmed alongside it, without deleting the original sentence.

The first broken link is separately recorded in DOC-41. Three things must be distinguished here: the page referenced by the execution record, the old link in the regular directory, and the replacement location itself. The execution record's page being 404 does not mean the old link in the regular directory is also absent; the old link still being readable does not mean the replacement location was written correctly either. Describing all three as a single "entry point anomaly" will cause subsequent rollback to target the wrong location.

When encountering this fork, first record "execution record page 404," then preserve the old entry point text, and then find an actual consumer. Until a consumer has been reached, do not treat the new entry point in the directory as grounds for retiring the old path. If only the old link in the directory is found, the recorded status is "directory readable, consumer not rechecked"; if the replacement location is found but the current revision has not been reached, it is still an incomplete migration record.

The early paragraphs that treated "the page opens" as a sufficient signal remain in the index. Later, only this point was revised: directory visibility does not prove adoption is complete. This correction explains why some rows list both a new maintenance location and callers that have not been rechecked, without updating all early rows to the same status.

## Change Only One Item per Confirmation

The approach in GMSC-005 is to change only the corresponding field after receiving confirmation. Confirmation about the maintenance location changes only the replacement location; confirmation about adoption scope changes only adoption scope; confirmation about exit responsibility also does not imply that the source assessments for both lock and license have been updated. This is not intended to split the index into finer pieces, but to prevent one reply from also marking callers that have not yet been checked as migrated.

After reviewing the existing implementation, the matter is passed to the current module maintainer. This handoff can be written alongside the associated source, but it cannot replace exit responsibility. The maintainer takes on handling the current module, not automatically the rollback conditions for all old entry points. The original record still preserves when the old entry point can be removed; new text at the replacement location must also still correspond to the specific source and adoption scope.

A record being maintained usually retains four sections of text: old entry point, replacement location, adoption scope, and exit responsibility. When an old assessment needs correcting, add a correction line after it rather than replacing it with an overview of unknown provenance. "Replacement location added" only means the new location contains text; only "caller verified" means an actual consumer has been traced; "can be removed" still depends on exit conditions. All three statements may be true at the same time, or only one may be true.

Independent schedules are not rewritten because a page name changes. Unconfirmed entries remain marked unconfirmed, even if another source has already migrated away. The index does not aim to organize every row into the same status; it aims to preserve how far each dependency source had progressed at that time.

## Treat the Adjacent Boundary Only as a Replay

GMSC-012 requires replaying the input with an adjacent integration-supply-boundary, while keeping the current entry point and original access path unchanged. Only then can the resulting difference still be attributed to the adjacent boundary that was replaced. This is not a second batch of caller migration: records for the old entry point, replacement location, and actual consumers are not changed during this pass.

Before the replay, the index leaves both entry points unchanged. After the replay, record only whether the adjacent boundary made the first difference occur earlier, later, or remain at the same point; leave cells without results blank rather than adding "no impact." If the result is the same as actual-consumer verification, preserve them separately as well. One keeps the entry point fixed and changes only the boundary; the other keeps the boundary fixed and finds consumers. They support different rollback assessments.

This section later entered review; an existing branch being complete only means the implementation is being reviewed, not that all callers have finished switching over. Handoff confirmation also only passes on the next stage of verification. The index must still record "replay performed" separately from "consumer verified" to prevent branch status from being misread as the adoption scope having narrowed.

## How to Document Restoring the Old Entry Point

The early rollback instructions consisted of just one sentence: restore the old entry point. That sentence is retained, but it does not explain which records remain valid after restoration. After restoring the entry point, check whether adoption records can still return to their original locations, whether verified callers read through the old entry point again, and whether corrections at the replacement location need to be marked as no longer used. Do not simply change the link back and then erase the differences that appeared in this batch.

Rollback does not touch sources that were not involved. A problem with the lock record does not automatically roll back the license record; a difference in the replay of one adjacent boundary also does not remove other entries with the same name. If the problem is only with the page referenced by the execution record, what is restored is the access entry point, not a dependency source fabricated to fill the gap. If the problem is with a field at the replacement location, the old entry point can continue to serve as a recovery point, while the new field remains pending recheck; it must not be disguised as an already verified old value.

The old index once used three conditions to prepare to stop maintaining the old path: the replacement location was readable, one caller confirmed it, and the old record remained readable. These conditions remain to help explain why early migration batches were preparing to close; they did not cover the 404 encountered later or consumers that had not been rechecked. Later additions preserve, at a minimum, the old entry point, the replacement location, and the location reached in the most recent trace of an actual consumer together. If any one is missing, the old path is not removed from the index.

## Reopening Old Records

When reopening a row later, read the dependency source first, then the row's old entry point and replacement location, and finally the caller column. Do not first use the filename to determine which batch it belongs to. If the caller column still says not rechecked, stop reading here; if it already records a first difference, return to that point to determine whether it was an entry point change, the page being 404, or different content at the replacement location.

This sequence also prevents a broken link from being treated as the status of the entire record. When the execution record's page does not open, preserve the old text first; when the replacement location opens but the caller has not reached the current revision, keep the not-rechecked status; restore the old entry point only when rolling back, and specify beside the original batch which location the restoration targets.

## Records Still Left in the Margins

Leave descriptions that cannot be rechecked unchanged; do not fill them in with results later confirmed for another source. An old entry point may have only its name left, or it may still be called; these two states must not be combined. Old and new assessments placed side by side, field-level updates, actual-consumer verification, and adjacent-boundary replay each remain in their own records; return to the corresponding row for whichever section has been checked.

Blank rows in the index also stay in their original positions. They may indicate that the replacement location has not yet been confirmed, or that the caller has not yet reached the first difference; until there is a new recheck, do not fill them with another row's conclusion.

This page still has outdated parts: it retains the old position that "directory visibility is enough to prepare to close," as well as callers that have not yet been checked individually. When new consumers are added later, append them only under the corresponding dependency source; do not rewrite old batches into conclusions learned only afterward.

# Release Automation: Legacy-to-Current Entry Point Migration Index

Legacy entry points did not become invalid just because current entry points appeared in the directory. This index was written based on the known usage relationships for `memory-release-automation` at the time. It records only legacy entry points, replacement locations, and callers still using the legacy entry points. Where callers could not be traced through the records, their names are left blank rather than filled in. The build queues, artifact versions, and rollback windows associated with `.github/workflows` are easy to lump into one row, but they have separate schedules, maintainers, and exit criteria.

To find a replacement location, first open `docs/adj-memory/migration/current entry point-legacy entry point migration index.md`, then follow the current entry points recorded there. This location holds only the index; the body text and attachments are still maintained by the memory · Release Automation project. Similarly named pages, alternate routes, and newly created directories are not automatically included in this record. Whether migration from a legacy entry point to a current one is complete must be checked with the actual callers, not judged by whether a new name already exists in the directory.

"Current" in this index means only the replacement location found at the time. It does not mean all users have switched or that the legacy entry point can be deleted. Build queues, artifact versions, and rollback windows each get their own row. If a caller touches two types of objects, record two rows as well; do not fill in one maintainer record from another. One item's schedule does not end early just because another item has already migrated. Do not fill blanks with guesses. Where something cannot be reconciled with the original record, leave the old description in place. Only when an actual user is identified later should it be added to the corresponding migration batch; leave earlier rows unchanged.

| Object to migrate | Legacy entry point column | Current entry point column |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Build queue | Callers still coming through the legacy entry point | The corresponding replacement location, and whether that caller has actually used it |
| Artifact version | Version records retained under the legacy entry point | Record the replacement location and caller separately; do not infer them from queue status |
| Rollback window | Callers that need to return to the legacy path | Keep the incomplete marker if the current entry point cannot yet replace the legacy path |

The migration sequence at the time:

1. Start with one actual caller and identify which type of object it touches. Do not start by bulk-changing directories or collapse all three objects into a single "migrated" status.
2. Once you have found the current entry point for that caller, have it use that entry point once. Finding a location in the directory only shows that the name exists in the index; it does not show that the caller has migrated off the legacy entry point.
3. If it does not work, leave the legacy entry point in place. Record where it broke and which caller was affected in that row. Another caller having completed the change is not enough to decide the status of this row.
4. Cross the legacy entry point off the index only after the caller is using the current entry point, the corresponding rollback window no longer needs the legacy path, and that object's own exit criteria have been met.

For rollback, first restore the legacy path for the affected caller. Keep the current entry point's entry and mark it incomplete. Whether other legacy entry points also needed to be restored had not been decided at the time; do not record one return to a legacy path as cancellation of the entire migration batch. A build queue switching entry points does not determine the status of artifact versions or rollback windows either.

This version does not include all callers. In particular, descriptions whose actual users could not be found in the available records retain their old wording. When adding information later, record legacy entry points, current entry points, and callers still using legacy entry points separately. Do not overwrite earlier migration batches with a single directory cleanup.

# memory · Release Automation Maintainer Map

Updates to `memory-release-automation` pass through `workflows` under `.github`, the resulting build queue, and artifact versions and withdrawal windows. The previous version had only a "Current contact" column, with no separate records for exit actions and temporary handoffs. Once someone picked up an exit action, readers could easily assume that the object had been fully handed over. This version keeps the original contact but separates temporary handoffs, exit actions, and long-term maintenance.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Receive an item for memory-release-automation] --> B{First check what it involves}
    B --> C[.github or workflows]
    B --> D[Build queue or artifact version]
    B --> E[Withdrawal window or exit action]
    B --> T[Temporary handoff action]
    C --> F[Project maintenance contact]
    D --> F
    E --> G[Temporary assignee]
    T --> F
    G --> H[Record only the exit action]
    F --> I{Long-term ownership confirmed}
    I -- Yes --> J[Enter the relevant maintainer]
    I -- No --> K[Leave blank]
```

The project maintenance contact in the diagram is not the overall owner. memory · Release Automation does not make technical determinations on behalf of long-term owners. It receives triage information within the scope of memory · Release Automation: the relevant `.github` location, workflow, build queue, artifact version, and whether a withdrawal window is involved. When the action at hand can be confirmed, route it to the relevant contact in the table; when the object's long-term technical meaning needs explaining, wait until long-term ownership is clear.

| Object at hand | First contact | What this route handles | Do not treat it as |
|---|---|---|---|
| `memory-release-automation` | memory · Release Automation maintenance contact | Determine whether the issue concerns a workflow, queue, artifact, or exit action | Long-term ownership of all objects |
| `.github` / `workflows` | Project maintenance contact | Record the workflow and build queue involved | A determination from GMS or enginetest |
| Build queue, artifact version | Project maintenance contact | Include the current artifact version and continue triage | A standing responsibility of the temporary assignee |
| Withdrawal window, exit action | Temporary assignee | Handle exit actions already handed to them | Long-term ownership of that object |
| Temporary handoff action | Project maintenance contact | Specify which action the handoff covers | Taking over all release automation |
| Long-term technical meaning | Relevant maintainer (blank if unconfirmed) | Add to the object's row once confirmed | Whoever replied most recently |
| Body and attachments | Project maintenance contact | Keep them maintained in the project materials | An archive location in an external project |

A blank is not an omission. Without long-term ownership, the temporary assignee is responsible only for exit actions already handed to them; having looked at a workflow or worked with a build queue does not turn that experience into long-term maintenance. Completing the actions within a withdrawal window only means that this exit action is finished.

GMS and enginetest are adjacent dependencies. When an issue requires their judgment, the contact listed here passes along only the objects and actions known on the memory side and does not fill in maintainers on their behalf.

### Filling in blanks

Once a long-term maintainer is confirmed, update only the relevant object's row; do not rewrite earlier records of temporary actions. State clearly whether the confirmed scope is a workflow, build queue, artifact version, or withdrawal window. A handoff covering only exit actions stays in the temporary handoff row and is not moved into long-term ownership of `memory-release-automation`. Add new information only to confirmed objects; do not expand a record of temporary handling into a maintenance relationship for the entire automation.

The project maintenance contact receives triage information, not ownership of all objects. Handoff details can include the `.github` location or workflow, whether a queue has already formed, and how the artifact version relates to the withdrawal window. If the scope is still unclear, leave the field blank and wait for ownership to become clear; short-term actions do not automatically become long-term responsibilities just because they recur.

If a temporary handoff covers only the withdrawal window, the record only needs to state the scope of the exit action. Do not copy that person's name into the object rows for `.github`, the build queue, or the artifact version; fill in each of those rows only after its maintainer is confirmed.

The maintenance contact still points to `docs/adj-memory/ownership/memory-release-automation-Current Maintainer Map.md`. This is a latest-known export of the memory · Release Automation knowledge base; the body and attachments are still maintained by the project. The field note from the first handoff gap remains at DOC-44; it preserves the gap as it stood then and does not supply unconfirmed long-term ownership for this map.

The initial draft's answer was "the person who found the entry point handles it first." This was temporary wording used at the time to keep the issue moving, not a confirmed responsibility. This sentence places three checks before closure; focused selectors is not a standalone completion criterion. The initial draft did not arrange the three items as sequential steps. # Sort and Window Execution Decision Record

The initial draft presented "retain the current statistics entry point" and "adjust the window" as two alternative paths, then stated that the latter would not be treated as a global switch for now. Review found that this wording could still easily conflate the entry point for finding material, execution scope, and compatibility judgments. This revision does not interpret the two phrases as new implementation designs; they were simply approaches compared at the meeting. There is only one decision to record: the sort and window execution rollout can proceed only within the specific scope covered by the existing material. It cannot be expanded into a full switchover merely because an entry point remains available, an adjacent issue looks similar, or an adjustment has been proposed.

This review at Northstar Data Systems established a narrow scope, not an overall owner for statistics, sort, or window. The existing material also did not expand "adjust the window" into specific changes, so this record retains the original name without supplying an object, timing, or implementation method for it. Retaining the two paths this way lets readers see what was compared at the time, without presenting anything not yet explained as a settled decision.

## Where the Decision Applies

This round did not select either "retain the current statistics entry point" or "adjust the window" as a global answer. The former can remain as a lead for review, and the latter can remain as a name for further discussion; neither automatically indicates that a particular schema or sorting compatibility question has passed.

Approval is granted by specific scope. Scope jointly supported by the existing material can be included in the rollout; scope with missing material, mismatched material, or inferences based only on adjacent scenarios remains on hold. Putting a scenario on hold is not a conclusion that it has failed; it only means that this decision has not included it in the scope of action. Any future expansion should also establish its own material for the additional scope, rather than interpreting an approved result as a default switch.

"Specific scope" here cannot be recorded merely as a sort or window label. At a minimum, the record should let reviewers distinguish whether the discussion concerns a particular schema issue or a particular sorting compatibility question, and why the three pieces of material belong to the same assessment. If the record uses only generic terms for sorting or windows, readers can neither tell whether the row result answers the same SQL nor identify which owner should receive the question. The initial draft did not make this interpretation clear; this revision adds it, but does not add any new implementation commitments as a result.

The rejected options and reasons for opposition included in the record remain. The material only says that they should remain part of this decision; it does not provide an itemized account of the reasons for opposition. This review has not filled those gaps with specific technical reasons; what can be settled now is the approval boundary, not a conclusion on every reservation.

The acceptance statement adopted at the meeting was:

> A query-engine decision is accepted only after a minimal SQL reproducer, analyzed-plan evidence, and the observable row result agree.

Here, agree requires all three pieces of material to address the same scope awaiting approval. The minimal SQL reproducer anchors the discussion to a reproducible statement; the analyzed-plan evidence corresponds to the plan being examined; and the row result allows the visible output after execution to be compared with the first two items. These are not three independent pieces of good news: if SQL points to one condition, the plan material points to another, or the row result does not fall within the same scope, they cannot be combined into a single approval. Conversely, agreement among the three pieces of material supports only that scope; it does not justify extending the conclusion to schema or sorting compatibility questions that have not yet been explained.

This record does not reproduce a particular SQL, a plan fragment, or a specific value in a row, because the retained material contains none of these examples. The requirement here is that the three actually align during review, not that the word "passed" stand in for them. Therefore, the absence of a particular schema's result from the body cannot be read as evidence that it has passed; likewise, unlisted scenarios have not been recorded as failures.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[Minimal SQL reproducer] --> D{Do all three pieces of material correspond to the same scope}
    B[analyzed plan evidence] --> D
    C[Row result] --> D
    D -->|Yes| E[Include in this round's approved scope]
    D -->|No or missing items| F[Keep on hold]
```

The diagram shows the decision relationship, not the sequence of a single execution. Material may be found through different entry points, but before it is included in the approved scope, it must be possible to bring it together around the same matter. The "Yes" in the diagram also does not assign a person to take on a particular question; complete technical material and someone taking responsibility for the question are two separate requirements retained in this round.

When reading this record, first identify the scope under discussion, then check whether the three pieces of material can be brought together for that scope, and finally confirm whether an owner is explicitly recorded for the corresponding schema or sorting compatibility question. Path names and file paths can only help readers access the material; they cannot supply the answers to these three judgments.

## The Two Paths Have Not Been Removed

The value of "retain the current statistics entry point" is that it leaves a known starting point for review. The initial draft put this point early on, which could easily be read as "keep using the entry point first, and the other judgments follow naturally." That implication has now been corrected: the entry point can remain, but conclusions must be confirmed individually; neither can substitute for the other. Here, statistics is an entry point being compared, not proof of schema and sorting compatibility, nor a source of ownership.

"Adjust the window" has not been judged to be an incorrect option. It was not adopted in this round because the retained material provided only this name, without explaining what would be adjusted, what scope it would cover, or how it should be understood alongside the current statistics entry point. Treating it directly as a rollout switch would bypass each scope's own SQL, plan, and row result. It therefore remains an unresolved path, not an implementation action that has already been scheduled.

The two paths retain their original names to avoid erasing the comparison made at the time, not to piece together a more complete rationale after the fact. The existence of reasons for opposition must remain here; their specific content was not retained with the material. This page does not recast unrecorded reservations as a particular execution failure, nor use them to claim that one side has been proven wrong.

The initial draft's statement "do not select adjust the window as a global switch for now" remains valid, but it must now be read alongside the other half: retaining the current statistics entry point is not a global switch either. The revision does not change sides between the two paths; it moves the subject of the decision from path names back to the scope covered by evidence. Further discussions may continue comparing the two paths, but they cannot bypass the acceptance conditions established in this round.

## Compatibility Questions Are Handed Off Individually

The exact wording in the meeting material was: downstream integrators need one owner for every schema and sorting compatibility question.

The emphasis in this sentence is every. Every schema issue raised and every sorting compatibility question must have an explicit owner; they cannot be left under a single vague umbrella merely because they all belong to the sort and window execution rollout. Conversely, which questions the same owner can take on must be stated clearly beside the questions themselves, rather than inferred backward from a test entry point, a statistics entry point, or a file location.

Accordingly, this round adopts recording an owner by question, rather than writing one name per file or per batch of rollout work. If a piece of material addresses both schema and sorting compatibility, the record must make it clear whether the same owner takes on both or they are assigned to different owners; without that explanation, it cannot be counted as handed off. The material provides no specific person or team names, so this decision does not make additional assignments or describe an unnamed person as the default recipient.

This requirement and the three pieces of technical material do not cancel each other out. Even if a scope already has a minimal SQL, plan material, and row result, the record must still state who handles the schema or sorting compatibility questions within it; conversely, recording an owner cannot replace the three pieces of material. Stating the owner clearly prevents technical conclusions from going unanswered; retaining the three pieces of material prevents a handoff name from replacing an actual assessment.

The owner in the record also does not mean transferring all technical judgments to one person. It answers only a narrower question: when downstream integrators raise a specific schema or sorting compatibility question, who takes it on. This record does not bind owners and approved scopes into one-to-one technical objects; whether an owner takes on multiple questions must be stated explicitly in the record, not inferred from shared terminology.

## Entry Points Retained During Review

This review looked back through `enginetest/enginetests.go` and call names such as sort, window, and execution. That path was the starting point for finding material at the time, not a permanent ownership assignment. Treating a file location as an owner would misread "where a lead was found" as "who must answer compatibility questions"; the decision to specify owners by question explicitly rules out that reading.

Likewise, statistics appears in the comparison of the two paths and therefore cannot be removed from the record; but that does not make it the point of adjudication for every sorting or window scenario. What this review accomplishes here is separating entry points from approval: entry points help locate the material from that time, while approval is still determined by SQL, plans, and row results that align within the same scope. No additional exceptions were made in this round for scope not covered by material.

This page therefore records entry points, material, approval, and owners separately. Entry points answer where to look back; material answers whether a scope has been supported; approval answers what can proceed in this round; owners answer who takes on compatibility questions. Collapsing all four into "statistics already exists, so rollout can proceed" loses two judgments at once: whether the three pieces of material align, and whether someone takes on every question.

Test files, minimal SQL, analyzed plans, and row results each serve different purposes. Test files provide an entry point for looking back; minimal SQL identifies the case to reproduce; plans and row results jointly support whether to accept that case. Even if they are part of the same discussion, one item cannot stand in for the other two. In particular, the mere appearance of sort and window near similar call names does not justify assuming that the two execution scenarios have reached the same conclusion.

## What Remains Unresolved

What "adjust the window" actually adjusts, the scope it involves, and its relationship to the current statistics entry point remain unspecified. The material also does not include a list of the actual owners for every schema and sorting compatibility question. Scope lacking three corresponding pieces of material remains on hold; the details of the original reasons for opposition have likewise not been restored.

These gaps determine where this page should stop: retain this round's conditional approval, retain the two paths that were not selected as global switches, and retain the requirement for an owner for each question. For follow-up records concerning the optimizer convergence window switchover handoff, see DOC-52; this page does not prematurely present material that has not yet been checked as a completed handoff.

Start with the call names near `enginetest/enginetests.go` to identify candidates for `memory-index`, then trace the old entry points each one uses. If either the consumer list or the rollback action is missing, keep the status as migration in progress. The candidate path is not the default entry point in this version, and it is not a basis for conclusions about compatible callers. Leave items whose return location is unclear on the old-entry-point side until the materials are complete enough to assess them. The list records only consumers already identified.

# Optimizer Convergence Window Handoff

Keep the old entry points in place when switching the convergence window. This does not move the entire optimizer to the candidate path. Instead, list the known consumers of `memory-index` one by one, confirm which old entry point each currently goes through, then pick one consumer that can be rolled back independently for a trial. Until the inventory is complete, the candidate path must not be expanded module-wide. Each newly discovered call site adds inventory work, not a completed migration.

The first draft started the search from `enginetest/enginetests.go` and nearby call names. That lead remains in the record so the start of the list can be found from the test side. Review narrowed its role: a location where a call name appears only indicates that further investigation is warranted; it does not prove that the consumer is already in the migration batch. File locations are also no substitute for an actual description of the planner or execution boundary.

## The Paths Did Not Move Together

```text
Before the switch
[Known memory-index consumers] ---> [Old entry points]

During the trial
[One independently reversible consumer] ---> [Candidate path]
[Other known consumers]                ---> [Old entry points]

Rollback
[That trial consumer]                  ---> [Old entry point]
```

The second line in the diagram represents just one trial consumer, not a second set of consumers. The remaining entries stay on the old-entry-point side, including callers whose compatibility has not yet been fully assessed. Rollback changes that consumer's routing; its inventory row, the reproducer from that time, and the open risks all remain. This lets readers distinguish between "a trial was run" and "the consumer has migrated."

## One Handoff Row

Give each known consumer its own row, in this order: old entry point, boundary, reproducer, evidence custodian, compatibility risk, rollback action. Do not combine several consumers into a single optimizer entry: the boundary, reproducer, and rollback would end up referring to different consumers.

> Every handoff names the affected planner or execution boundary, the exact reproducer, the current evidence owner, and the compatibility risk still open.

For the boundary, specify the affected planner or execution side; do not substitute a module name. For the reproducer, give the specific input or steps that bring that consumer back to the state underlying the assessment. If no usable reproducer is available, mark it as missing. The evidence custodian is the person who holds the evidence for that instance, not a component name. Compatibility risks should list only caller conditions that have not been ruled out; they may remain open after the trial ends. A complete handoff row must also specify which old entry point the consumer returns to. "Can be rolled back" is not an action.

All six fields must refer to the same consumer. Having a reproducer does not mean it can be switched, and having an old entry point does not mean it can be rolled back. Conversely, if an entry lists a return action but does not describe the boundary, the person taking over cannot tell whether rollback returns it to the original planner or execution side. If the consumer inventory, old entry point, or rollback action is missing, keep the record marked as migration in progress.

## Two Labels in the Inventory

Keep both "known consumer" and "eligible for trial" labels in the inventory. The former answers who still uses the old entry points; the latter answers only whether a consumer can be rolled back independently in this round. Neither label can replace the other. A consumer Fang Ke may already have been identified and have a clearly documented boundary, yet remain only in the first category because compatibility callers have not yet been assessed. Conversely, completing a trial does not remove it from the known-consumer list.

When evidence changes hands, first check which row the reproducer still corresponds to, then update the evidence custodian. Do not borrow a reproducer from another consumer to fill a gap. That would make the candidate path look reversible while leaving the record unclear about which old entry point to return to.

## Leave Compatibility Entries Where They Are

List compatibility callers individually in the original consumer's risk field; do not draw them as separate migrated entities. They continue to use the old entry points in this round until their relationship to the trial consumer can be explained. If a compatibility caller merely appears near the same call name, treat it as an item to investigate. It cannot replace the trial consumer's boundary or reproducer.

Rolling back the trial consumer restores only that consumer. The old entry points therefore remain the compatibility paths for the other consumers, rather than a temporary note. To expand the scope next time, select another independently reversible entry from the inventory and write a new handoff row. Do not treat the previous round's candidate path as automatic approval. If a rollback action depends on another consumer, it does not qualify as independently reversible here and must stay on the old-entry-point side.

## From Inventory to Trial

First inventory the known consumers of `memory-index`. "Known" here means only consumers already identified; it is not an estimate of all potential callers. For each newly discovered entry, first add its old entry point and affected boundary to its own row. If evidence changes hands, update only the custodian; do not close compatibility risks along with it.

Then select just one independently reversible consumer to take the candidate path. Before it enters, its row needs reproducible input or steps, the person holding the evidence, the open compatibility risks, and an explicit action for returning to the old entry point. All other known consumers continue to use the old entry points. The candidate path thus defines only the scope of this trial, not a default judgment about similar callers.

When the trial needs to stop, restore the selected consumer's route through the previously documented old entry point. Do not delete the inventory row or erase the candidate path from the record; keeping them makes it possible to see where the trial took place and where the consumer was restored. Entries without an independent rollback action stay on the old-entry-point side, even if their boundaries and reproducers are complete.

## Simplified Steps Retained from the First Draft

The first draft built a candidate list from call names before filling in the old entry points. That sequence is no longer used to assess trial eligibility, but it is retained because it explains why the list started from the `enginetest/enginetests.go` side. The old entry point is now documented before deciding whether to run a trial. Call names can help find items to investigate; they cannot substitute for consumers, boundaries, or rollback relationships.

For the actual entry point for statistics identity migration, see DOC-53. It is adjacent to the window switch when looking things up, but is not included in this page's trial batch. Three points remain unresolved on this page: the complete list of consumers corresponding to the old entry points, the compatibility callers involved with the trial consumer, and the specific reproducer evidence that should remain with the record after rollback.

# optimizer-sets entry-point retrace

This route was left for whoever was taking over the statistics identity migration at the time. Start at the repository's public optimizer-sets, rather than working backward from every file with statistics in its name. That approach mixes same-name landmarks with actual calls and can also lead to treating `sql/statistics.go` as the migration's permanent home.

The route mapped out at the time retained only three locations: `optimizer-sets`, one direct caller, and the first actual consumer of the statistics identity migration. Do not reverse this order. The entry point, caller, and consumer must connect; matching just one of those terms does not mean you have found this path.

First, identify the adjacent direct caller at the entry point of optimizer-sets. This deliberately follows only one hop: the goal is to find who actually receives this information, not to expand every location in the optimizer where sets appears. When you encounter a file with the same name, first ask whether this call edge leads to it; without that relationship, treat it only as a landmark. In particular, do not replace the path you have already found based on a filename just because `sql/statistics.go` also contains similar names.

Next, follow that caller to the first actual consumer. When retracing, distinguish "a search hit for identity" from "consuming identity": a same-name hit can make the search stop too soon; this page stops only where the consumer receives the migration. "First" here also reflects the scope at the time, not an assignment of ownership for subsequent processing. If what you are reading has already gone beyond this consumer, bring the notes back to its entry point rather than tracing further.

An analyzed plan capture was saved alongside this route. It was used to align the entry point, the direct caller, and the location reached at the time; the capture alone cannot substitute for the call relationship. If the capture does not match the location you are reading, first go back and check the link between optimizer-sets and that caller. Do not jump to same-name statistics results and map everything out again.

Read the capture together with the entry point and caller. With only the plan location and neither of those reference points, someone coming later could confuse it with a same-name route.

The old note called optimizer-sets the "actual entry point." That wording refers only to where this retrace began; it does not mean that sets defines statistics identity or that `sql/statistics.go` is the only location. This page records the point reached at the time by following that file and call name; the file location is not a permanent home. The old wording is retained to avoid inferring migration ownership from a filename.

The route ends at the first consumer. What processing identity goes through after that, and which location is responsible for it, are questions for another owner; this page does not fill in that stretch with a conclusion. To locate it again, first retrace this one direct caller, then compare it with the saved capture.
